And may the blessed Trinity and all the saints keep and defend thee from all evils; and God give thee grace to do His will always, so that He be honoured in thee, and that thou and I may both, after this mortal life is ended, be with Him together, and praise Him everlastingly. Amen.
q.w: Teachings to his son Philip (Enseignements), in Joinville's Life of St. Louis
q.l: Joinville's Chronicle, St. Lewis falls sick: his instructions to his son (closing blessing)

q.t: I pray thee to make thyself beloved of the people of thy kingdom; for truly I would rather that a Scot should come out of Scotland and govern the people of the kingdom well and equitably than that thou shouldest govern it ill in the sight of all men.
q.w: Sayings recorded by Joinville in his Life of St. Louis
q.l: Joinville's Chronicle, First Book: principal virtues of St. Lewis (to his eldest son Louis, in sickness at Fontainebleau)

q.t: Keep yourself then from knowingly doing or saying anything which, if the whole world heard thereof, you would be ashamed to acknowledge
q.w: Sayings recorded by Joinville in his Life of St. Louis
q.l: Joinville's Chronicle, First Book: principal virtues of St. Lewis

q.t: For you should know that there is no leprosy so hideous as the being in mortal sin, inasmuch as the soul that is in mortal sin is like unto the Devil; wherefore no leprosy can be so hideous.
q.w: Sayings recorded by Joinville in his Life of St. Louis
q.l: Joinville's Chronicle, First Book: St. Lewis's horror of sin

q.t: you should never disdain what God did for our teaching. So I pray you, for the love of God first, and then for the love of me, that you accustom yourself to wash the feet of the poor.
q.w: Sayings recorded by Joinville in his Life of St. Louis
q.l: Joinville's Chronicle, First Book: St. Lewis's love for the poor (on the Maundy Thursday washing of feet)

q.t: So ought you to believe all the articles of the faith, to which the Apostles have borne witness, as also you chant of a Sunday in the Creed.
q.w: Sayings recorded by Joinville in his Life of St. Louis
q.l: Joinville's Chronicle, First Book: what St. Lewis thought about faith

q.t: Let us therefore take the warning that God has given us in such sort that, if we feel that we have, in our hearts or bodies, anything displeasing to God, we shall remove it hastily; and if there be anything we think will please Him, let us try hastily to do it. If we so act, then our Lord will give us blessings in this world, and in the next blessings greater than we can tell.
q.w: Sayings recorded by Joinville in his Life of St. Louis
q.l: Joinville's Chronicle, First Book: the warnings of God, how they are to be turned to advantage

q.t: Therefore I like better to place my own person, and my wife, and my children in God's hands than do this harm to the many people who are here.
q.w: Sayings recorded by Joinville in his Life of St. Louis
q.l: Joinville's Chronicle, the king's ship strikes off Cyprus on the voyage home (refusing to abandon the ship)

q.t: I would consent to be branded with a hot iron on condition that all profane oaths were removed out of my realm.
q.w: Sayings recorded by Joinville in his Life of St. Louis
q.l: Joinville's Chronicle, horror of St. Lewis for all blasphemy

q.t: My faultles brest the fornace is, the fuell woundinge thornes, Love is the fire, and sighes the smoke, the ashes shame and scornes ; The fuell Justice layeth on, and Mercy blowes the coales, The mettall in this fornace wrought are men's defiléd soules
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: With teares He fightes and wynnes the feild, His naked breste standes for a sheilde, His battering shott are babishe cryes, His arrowes, lookes of weepinge eyes, His martiall ensignes, colde and neede, And feeble fleshe His warrier's steede.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: Gift better then Him self God doth not knowe, Gift better then his God no man can see ; This gift doth here the giver given bestowe, Gift to this gift lett ech receiver bee : God is my gift, Him self He freely gave me, God's gift am I, and none but God shall have me.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: They sawe, they harde, they felt Him sitting nere, Unseene, unfelt, unhard, they Him receivd ; No diverse thinge, though divers it appeare ; Though sences faile, yet faith is not deceiv'd ; And if the wonder of the worke be newe, Beleive the worke because His worde is trewe.
q.w: Of the Blessed Sacrament of the Aulter
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: Christe's final meale was fountayne of our good, For mortall meate He gave immortall foode. That which He gaue, He was: O peerelesse gifte ! Both God and man He was, and both He gaue.
q.w: Of the Blessed Sacrament of the Aulter
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: Not allwayes fall of leafe nor ever springe, No endlesse night yet not eternall daye ; The saddest birdes a season finde to singe, The roughest storme a calme may soone alaye ; Thus with succeding turnes God tempereth all, That man may hope to rise yet feare to fall.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: Man's soule of endles bewtye's image is, Drawen by the worke of endles skill and might ; This skillfull might gave many sparkes of blisse, And to descerne this blisse a native light ; To frame God's image as His worthes requird, His might, His skill, His worde and will conspir'd.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: In lowly vales I mounte To Pleasure's highest pitch ; My sely shroud trew honors bringes, My poore estate is ritch. My conscience is my crowne, Contented thoughts my rest ; My hart is happy in it selfe, My blisse is in my breste.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: Avaunt, O viper! I thy spite defye : There is a God that overrules thy force, Who can thy weapons to His will applie, And shorten or prolonge our brittle course. I on His mercy, not thy might, relye ; To Him I live, for Him I hope to die.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: Thus still I dye, yet still I do revive ; My living death by dying life is fedd ; Grace more then nature kepes my hart alive, Whose idle hopes and vayne desires are deade. Not where I breath, but where I love, I live ; Not where I love, but where I am, I die ; The life I wish, must future glory give, The deaths I feele in present daungers lye.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: O soule! do not thy noble thoughtes abase, To loose thy loves in any mortall wight ; Content thy eye at home with native grace, Sith God Himself is ravisht with thy sight ; If on thy bewty God enamored be, Base be thy love of any lesse then He.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: To beautye's fading blisse I am no thrall ; I bury not my thoughtes in mettall mynes ; I ayme not at such fame as feareth fall ; I seeke and finde a light that ever shynes
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: O mylde and mightye Lorde! Amend that is amisse ; My synn my sore, Thy love my salve, Thy cure my comfort is. Confirme Thy former deede, Reforme that is defild ; I was, I am, I will remayne Thy charge, Thy choise, Thy childe.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: Butt Mercye may relente, And temper Justice' rodd, For mercy doth as much belonge As justice to a Godd.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: Christ ! health of feuer'd soule, heauen of the mind, Force of the feeble, nurse of infant loues, Guide to the wandring foote, light to the blind, Whom weeping winnes, repentant sorrow moues ; Father in care, mother in tender hart, Reuiue and saue me, slaine with sinnefull dart !
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: I dare not say, I will, but wish I may; My pride is checkt, high words the speaker spilt. My good, O Lord, Thy gift, Thy strength my stay! Give what Thou bidst, and then bid what Thou wilt. Worke with me what Thou of me doos't request, Then will I dare the most and vow the best.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: Gemm to her worth, spouse to her love ascendes, Prince to her throne, queene to her heavenly Kinge, Whose court with solemne pompe on her attends, And quires of saintes with greeting notes do singe; Earth rendreth upp her undeserved praye, Heaven claymes the right, and beares the prize awaye.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: O sacred fire ! come shewe thy force on me, That sacrifice to Christe I maye retorne : If withered wood for fuell fittest bee, If stones and dust, yf fleshe and bloode will burne, I withered am, and stonye to all good, A sacke of dust, a masse of fleshe and bloode.
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: O trewe life! sith Thou hast left me, Mortall life is tedious ; Death it is to live without Thee, Death of all most odious : Turne againe or take me to Thee, Let me dye or live Thou in me!
q.w: Mary Magdalen's Complaint at Christ's Death
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: Christ Himselfe, by making a hymne the conclusion of His Last Supper, and the prologue to the first pageant of His Passion, gaue His Spouse a methode to imitate, as in the office of the Church it appeareth; and to all men a patterne, to know the true vse of this measured and footed stile.
q.w: The Author to his Louing Cosin (prose preface to Saint Peter's Complaint)
q.tr: written in English; ed. A. B. Grosart

q.t: And I dare well say to the sinner, be he never so wicked in his living, if at any time in this life he will be penitent for it and desire forgiveness and mercy of Almighty God, He of His great goodness will sooner forgive him than all the water in the sea can quench one spark of fire, if it were cast upon it
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Second Penitential Psalm (Psalm 31/32), vol. I p. 36
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: Weeping doeth that thing in the soul which rubbing and fretting doeth in the iron. Rubbing taketh away rust and cankering from the iron. And weeping putteth away from the soul the infection of sin. The iron with rubbing anon will shine full bright. So the soul with weeping is made fair and white.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: First Penitential Psalm (Psalm 6), vol. I p. 14
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: By the virtue of contrition our sins be forgiven ; by confession they be forgotten ; but by satisfaction they be so clean done away that no sign or token remaineth in any condition of them, but as clean as ever we were.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Second Penitential Psalm (Psalm 31/32), vol. I p. 21
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: let us appear and shew ourself even as we be. Truly all we be sinners, for if we say no sin is in us, we condemn ourself and say not truth : therefore let us shew ourself as sinners.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Second Penitential Psalm (Psalm 31/32), vol. I p. 27
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: Peter offended grievously in denying his Master, Christ. Paul in pursuing His Church. Mary Magdalene sinned grievously in misusing the pleasures of her body ; and many other without number were sinners, almost so many as now be saints in Heaven. There is no saint in Heaven (a few excepted) but, ere they came there, had need some time to ask of Almighty God the gift of contrition.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Second Penitential Psalm (Psalm 31/32), vol. I p. 29
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: The virtue and strength of the grace of God is marvellous, that where it once pierceth and entereth into the soul of any creature, it maketh him bold and to hope well, in so much that he dare make battle afresh against his enemies.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: First Penitential Psalm (Psalm 6), vol. I p. 17
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: O most holy Virgin, thou art the Mother of God, Mother of mercy, the Mother also of wretched sinners and their singular help, comfort to all sorrowful; vouchsafe to hear our wretchedness and provide a convenient and behovable remedy for the same.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Third Penitential Psalm (Psalm 37/38), Part I (sermon for the Nativity of Our Lady), vol. I p. 44
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: Therefore sith we have so good and many just causes both of hope and dread, (as me seemeth) he taketh the most sure way that maketh the one meet with the other : that is to say, hope with dread and dread with hope.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Fourth Penitential Psalm (Psalm 50/51), Part II, vol. I p. 98
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: So that now nothing may be more certain to us than it which is taught by Holy Church. No means may be found so speedful and ready to prove the certainty of anything concerning our faith as that the Church hath so affirmed and ordained. The Church of God may in no wise beguile in those things that belongeth to our faith and to the undoubtful health of the soul.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Fourth Penitential Psalm (Psalm 50/51), Part I, vol. I p. 93
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: And as often as the holy sacraments be iterated and used according to the commandment of Christ's Church, so often is the blessed Blood of our Lord sprinkled abroad to cleanse and put away sin.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Fourth Penitential Psalm (Psalm 50/51), Part I, vol. I p. 95
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: But Almighty God hath ordained more even laws, which be common both to poor and rich; He desireth none other sacrifice but such as the poor may do as soon as the rich, and peradventure more soon, for Almighty God taketh more heed to the good intent of the mind than to the greatness or value of the gift.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Fourth Penitential Psalm (Psalm 50/51), Part II, vol. I p. 112
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: Almighty God the high Artificer useth many divers means to shape and square His stones here in the earth, in His Church Militant. He of His goodness would every man and woman should be quick stones made ready for that heavenly building; His will is every creature to be saved, as St. Paul saith.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Fourth Penitential Psalm (Psalm 50/51), Part II, vol. I p. 116
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: The life of man is here but for a while, shortly it shall perish and be at an end; no space, no void time, no leisure can be had but always it draweth to an end; it cannot be at a point, it is never at rest, truly, one minute of an hour. Whether we eat or drink, wake or sleep, laugh or weep, ever our life here draweth to an end.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Fifth Penitential Psalm (Psalm 101/102), Part I, vol. II p. 8
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: The least Christian person, the poorest and most low in degree, is nigh in kindred to Almighty God; he is His son and His heir of the Kingdom of Heaven, brother unto Jesus Christ and bought with His precious Blood
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Fifth Penitential Psalm (Psalm 101/102), Part I, vol. II p. 21
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: So, good Lord, do now in like manner again with Thy Church Militant, change and make the soft and slippery earth into hard stones, set in Thy Church strong and mighty pillars that may suffer and endure great labours, watchings, poverty, thirst, hunger, cold and heat, which also shall not fear the threatenings of princes, persecution neither death
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Fifth Penitential Psalm (Psalm 101/102), Part II, vol. II p. 37
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: The more that our prayer is grounded in charity, the sooner it shall be heard of Him Whose commandment is all charity.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Fifth Penitential Psalm (Psalm 101/102), Part II, vol. II p. 30
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: This spiritual bread, the word of God, maketh the soul to be full of juice, full of the liquor of good devotion ; and also it maketh the soul strong and hardy to withstand all tribulations.
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Fifth Penitential Psalm (Psalm 101/102), Part I, vol. II p. 11
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: Who is now so stubborn and evil-willed that his heart could not melt and be kindled with the fire of charity, if he might hear the Apostles preach, see the constant faith of martyrs, and have at hand the holy conversations of confessors?
q.w: Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms (ed. J. S. Phillimore, 1914)
q.l: Fifth Penitential Psalm (Psalm 101/102), Part II, vol. II p. 51
q.tr: written in English; ed. J. S. Phillimore

q.t: For it is more splendid than gold, brighter than silver, more resplendent than the carbuncle, clearer than crystal, richer than topaz, and on the authority of him who speaks wisdom, all precious things are not to be compared with it. What, beloved brother, can youth more properly seek or age more soberly enjoy than the knowledge of the Holy Scriptures?
q.w: Letter to Nithard (Kylie letter II; MGH Epp. III no. 9)

q.t: I beseech your holy clemency with my most earnest entreaties, that you should deign to remember me in your holy prayers, and seek to make secure in a harbourage of unshakeable rock the ship of my mind buffeted by the waves of many storms among the people of Germany
q.w: Letter to Nothelm, Archbishop of Canterbury (Kylie letter X; MGH Epp. III no. 33)

q.t: all of us become in baptism sons and daughters of Christ and the Church, and thereby brothers and sisters.
q.w: Letter to Nothelm, Archbishop of Canterbury (Kylie letter X; MGH Epp. III no. 33)

q.t: May the Eternal God, who rewards just deeds, grant that my dearest sister rejoice in the celestial choir of the angels, for by sending a gift of scriptural books she has consoled with spiritual light an exile in Germany, who must trace dark and unfrequented places among the German nations, and who, unless he have the word of God as a lamp unto his feet, and a light unto his path, will fall into the snare of death.
q.w: Letter to Eadburga, Abbess of Thanet (Kylie letter XV; MGH Epp. III no. 30)

q.t: And through Him we beg you with the most earnest prayers, to intercede for us that the merciful Consoler of those in sorrow may deign to keep our souls, amid such storms, unharmed and safe from sin.
q.w: Letter to Daniel, Bishop of Winchester (Kylie letter XXVI; MGH Epp. III no. 63)

q.t: That you may not be ignorant of the cause of this prayer, know that because of our sins the course of our mission is threatened by many storms. Everywhere toil, everywhere sorrow.
q.w: Letter to Eadburga, Abbess of Thanet (Kylie letter XXVIII; MGH Epp. III no. 65)

q.t: We beg you, also, to intercede for the German peoples given over to the worship of idols, asking the Lord, who poured out His own blood for the safety of the whole world, and " will have all men to be saved and to come unto the knowledge of the truth," to turn them to a knowledge of the Creator and to the bosom of Mother Church.
q.w: Letter to Abbot Aldhere (Kylie letter XXXIII; MGH Epp. III no. 38)

q.t: The tribulations of this world despise with all the strength of thy mind, because all the soldiers of Christ, men and women, have looked down upon the storms and tribulations and infirmities of this life, and held them as nothing
q.w: Letter to Abbess Bugga (Kylie letter XXIX; MGH Epp. III no. 94)

q.t: He it is who in thy old age desires to decorate and adorn the fair beauty of thy soul with toil and tribulation. Rejoicing then, beloved, in the hope of thy future inheritance in thy heavenly home, to all adversities that assail thy heart or body, oppose the shield of faith and patience
q.w: Letter to Abbess Bugga (Kylie letter XXIX; MGH Epp. III no. 94)

q.t: We commend ourselves to your prayers, that whether in life or in death we may be united with the fellowship of your love.
q.w: Letter to Abbot Aldhere (Kylie letter XXXIII; MGH Epp. III no. 38)

q.t: Keep in mind the holy apostles and prophets: because they laboured much in the Lord, therefore have they gained eternal rewards.
q.w: Letter to Lioba, Tecla, Cynehilda and their sisters (Kylie letter XXXVI; MGH Epp. III no. 67)

q.t: As many as we draw by good example to the life of the heavenly kingdom, or lead to perdition by bad example, for so many, beyond a doubt, we shall receive either punishment or reward from the Eternal Judge.
q.w: Letter of Boniface and his fellow bishops to Æthelbald, King of the Mercians (Kylie letter XL; MGH Epp. III no. 73)

q.t: For examples in this connection we have the early Fathers Clement and Cornelius and several others in the city of Rome, Cyprian in Carthage, Athanasius in Alexandria, who under pagan emperors steered the ship of Christ, nay His beloved spouse, that is the Church, by teaching, and by struggling, and toiling and suffering even to the shedding of their blood.
q.w: Letter to Cuthbert, Archbishop of Canterbury (Kylie letter XLII; MGH Epp. III no. 78)

q.t: Let us stand fast in justice, and prepare our souls against temptation, that we may have the support of God and may say to him: " Lord, Thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations."
q.w: Letter to Cuthbert, Archbishop of Canterbury (Kylie letter XLII; MGH Epp. III no. 78)

q.t: For the apostle calls a priest of the Church overseer, the prophet calls him watchman, and the Saviour of the world calls him shepherd
q.w: Letter to Cuthbert, Archbishop of Canterbury (Kylie letter XLII; MGH Epp. III no. 78)

q.t: I bid thee, beloved, with regard to this slave Athalhere, if any need befalls him in this case, to aid him as thou shouldst a free man, and to speak for him to his friends as for a free man, not a slave.
q.w: Letter to the priest Denehard (Kylie letter XLIV; MGH Epp. III no. 99)

q.t: Fare thee well; mayst thou live as a virgin the true angelic life and with good repute reign eternally in heaven with Christ.
q.w: Letter to Eadburga, Abbess of Thanet, on the vision at Wenlock (Kylie letter XIII; MGH Epp. III no. 10)

q.t: When we rise up in the morning each day let us think that we shall not abide until the evening, and when we come to lie down also let us think that we shall not abide until the morning; for we know not the days of our life, but they are known unto God.
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men, no. 471

q.t: A man's life or death cometh from his neighbour; if we benefit our brother we benefit ourselves, and if we offend him we sin against God.
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men, no. 33

q.t: That which I command thee observe. Set thou God before thine eyes continually, wheresoever thou goest; whatsoever thou doest make to it a witness (or testimony) from the Scriptures; and in whatsoever place thou dwellest be not easily moved therefrom, but abide therein persistently. Observe these three things, and thou shalt be saved.
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men, no. 35

q.t: Put no confidence in thine own righteousness, and regret not nor cogitate upon a matter which is past, and be persistent in restraining thy tongue and thy belly.
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men, no. 197 (answer to Abba Pambo)

q.t: Let us put God before our eyes continually; remember death and Christ our Redeemer; hate the world and everything which is therein; hate the world and all bodily pleasure; die unto this life, so that thou mayest live unto God, for God will require it of thee in the day of judgement.
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men, no. 208

q.t: There are some monks who vex their bodies with the labours of abstinence and self-denial, and who, because they have not found understanding, are remote from the path of God.
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book I, Chapter VIII (Of scrupulous watchfulness in our thoughts and words and deeds), no. 296

q.t: The greatest might of a man is to bring upon his soul his transgression at all times before God, and he must expect temptation until the end.
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men, no. 368

q.t: It is not seemly for us to remember the time which hath passed, but let a man be each day as one who beginneth his toil, so that the excessive weariness [which we shall feel] may be to our advantage.
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book I, Chapter VIII (Of scrupulous watchfulness in our thoughts and words and deeds), no. 384

q.t: There are many who fall and who rise up to an attitude of rectitude, but there are some who fall from good deeds to polluted things; better is he who falleth and riseth up than he who standeth and then falleth.
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book I, Chapter XII (Of the acceptance of repentance), no. 607

q.t: A storm rose up against a ship on the sea, and destroyed the freight which she carried, but with the greatest difficulty she was saved [and brought] to land. Now what do ye wish to do? Do ye wish to drown him that hath been saved?
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book I, Chapter XII (Of the acceptance of repentance), no. 606 (message to the monks who refused a penitent brother)

q.t: As a fish when it is lifted up out of the water dieth, even so doth the monk who tarrieth outside his cell.
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book I, Chapter I (Of flight from men, and of silent contemplation, and of dwelling continually in the cell), no. 20

q.t: Behold a time shall come to the children of men when they shall become silly, and they shall turn aside and depart from the fear of God, and if they see a man who is neither as mad nor as silly as they are, they shall rise up against him, saying, 'Thou art both mad and silly,' because he is not like unto them.
q.w: The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. II (Sayings of the Fathers)
q.l: Book II, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life of the Holy Men, no. 179

q.t: That we should possess anything besides Christ is unnecessary, and we should not esteem anything of value besides the love of Christ, neither possessions nor kinsfolk, not even our soul itself.
q.w: The Life of Saint Anthony, by Athanasius (Syriac version), in The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. I
q.l: Life of St. Anthony, his teaching to those who came to him (Vol. I, p. 19)

q.t: Be ye afraid neither of sounds (or voices) nor of phantoms of this kind, for in this wise the devils are wont to act towards those who are timid; but seal ye yourselves with the Seal of the Cross, and return ye unto your homes in confidence, and forgive those who would make of you laughing-stocks.
q.w: The Life of Saint Anthony, by Athanasius (Syriac version), in The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. I
q.l: Life of St. Anthony, his admonition to visitors at his dwelling (Vol. I, p. 18)

q.t: So therefore, O my beloved, life is in our own hands to gain, for it is within us, and it is ministered unto by us.
q.w: The Life of Saint Anthony, by Athanasius (Syriac version), in The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. I
q.l: Life of St. Anthony, discourse to the monks (Vol. I, p. 21)

q.t: Let us, however, be not afraid of their stirrings, and let us not be made lax by reason of their blandishments (or flatteries); but let us be constant in fasting and in prayer, and straightway they shall be vanquished and disappear.
q.w: The Life of Saint Anthony, by Athanasius (Syriac version), in The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. I
q.l: Life of St. Anthony, discourse to the monks (Vol. I, p. 23)

q.t: Whensoever we make our life and deeds better than they were before, we increase the pleasure which we give to God, and we also multiply the contempt which we have for the evil ones.
q.w: The Life of Saint Anthony, by Athanasius (Syriac version), in The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. I
q.l: Life of St. Anthony, discourse to the monks (Vol. I, p. 26)

q.t: let us pray, not that we may know secret things, but that we may please the Divine Majesty, and that power may be given unto us to stand against the darts of the Evil One.
q.w: The Life of Saint Anthony, by Athanasius (Syriac version), in The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Vol. I
q.l: Life of St. Anthony, discourse to the monks (Vol. I, p. 28)

q.t: There is no one but would be willing to stand on Mount Thabor and see Christ transfigured ; but to go up to Jerusalem, and accompany Christ to Mount Calvary, few are willing.
q.w: Letters of St. Philip Neri (in Bacci, The Life of Saint Philip Neri, vol. II)
q.l: Letter I, to Messer Francesco Vai, Prato (Rome, November 6, 1556)

q.t: Spiritual persons are wont to have first sweetness, then bitterness; lay aside then this tepidity of yours; drop the mask, take hold of the cross, and let not the cross take hold of you.
q.w: Letters of St. Philip Neri (in Bacci, The Life of Saint Philip Neri, vol. II)
q.l: Letter I, to Messer Francesco Vai, Prato (Rome, November 6, 1556)

q.t: Besides this, be prudent, and not troublesome to anybody; take care that others may rather have of yours than you of theirs, because a spiritual man must rather give than have
q.w: Letters of St. Philip Neri (in Bacci, The Life of Saint Philip Neri, vol. II)
q.l: Letter I, to Messer Francesco Vai, Prato (Rome, November 6, 1556)

q.t: Pray for me, as I will do for you. And let us so live that though we cannot meet again in this life, we may meet in the other for ever, with that delight which the saints who are in Paradise are enjoying this very day.
q.w: Letters of St. Philip Neri (in Bacci, The Life of Saint Philip Neri, vol. II)
q.l: Letter X, to Madonna Fiora Ragni, Naples (Rome, April 15, 1580)

q.t: All created things are generous, and show the goodness of the Creator; the sun sheds light, the fire heat, every tree extends its arms, which are its boughs, and yields us the fruit which it produces, and the water and the air, and all nature shows forth the liberality of the Creator.
q.w: Letters of St. Philip Neri (in Bacci, The Life of Saint Philip Neri, vol. II)
q.l: Letter XIII, to Sister Anna Maria Trievi, Florence (Rome, August 30, 1585)

q.t: Take delight in the community life, avoid all singularity, give heed to purity of heart; for the Holy Spirit abides in candid and simple souls, and He is the master of prayer, and makes us dwell in constant peace and joy, which is a foretaste of Paradise
q.w: Letters of St. Philip Neri (in Bacci, The Life of Saint Philip Neri, vol. II)
q.l: Letter XIII, to Sister Anna Maria Trievi, Florence (Rome, August 30, 1585)

q.t: The long and short of it is, without Christ you can never have any good thing which is really good.
q.w: Letters of St. Philip Neri (in Bacci, The Life of Saint Philip Neri, vol. II)
q.l: Letter XVII, a fragment, to Tiberio

q.t: To acquire the love of God, there is no truer and shorter way than to detach ourselves from the things of the world, even small and trifling things, and from self-love
q.w: Letters of St. Philip Neri (in Bacci, The Life of Saint Philip Neri, vol. II)
q.l: Letter XXIII, to Sister Anna Maria Trievi, Florence (Rome, April 29, 1594)

q.t: as the ship which has a sufficient depth of water sails more securely through it as it ploughs its way along, so also I am persuaded that by the sacrifices and prayers of a number of persons I shall arrive more happily and easily at the port of life eternal, when it shall please the Lord to call me.
q.w: Letters of St. Philip Neri (in Bacci, The Life of Saint Philip Neri, vol. II)
q.l: Letter XIX, to the Blessed Giovenale Ancina, Naples (Rome, May 10, 1591)

q.t: My son, persevere in your cheerfulness, for this is the true way to advance in every virtue.
q.w: The Life of Saint Philip Neri, by Father Bacci (sayings of the Saint)
q.l: Book II, Chapter VII (Philip's wonderful way of keeping young people from vice)

q.t: Let them talk; go you on with your play, and be merry; all I want of you is to keep out of the way of sin.
q.w: The Life of Saint Philip Neri, by Father Bacci (sayings of the Saint)
q.l: Book II, Chapter VII (Philip's wonderful way of keeping young people from vice)

q.t: Lord! beware of me to-day, lest I should betray Thee, and do all the evil in the world.
q.w: The Life of Saint Philip Neri, by Father Bacci (sayings of the Saint)
q.l: Book II, Chapter XVII (Of Philip's humility)

q.t: Only give me ten truly detached men, and I do not despair of converting the world with them.
q.w: The Life of Saint Philip Neri, by Father Bacci (sayings of the Saint)
q.l: Book II, Chapter XV (Of Philip's detachment from worldly goods)

q.t: Throw yourselves into God's hands, and be sure that if He wants anything of you, He will give you all that is needful for the purpose for which He wishes to use you.
q.w: The Life of Saint Philip Neri, by Father Bacci (sayings of the Saint)
q.l: Book II, Chapter XVII (Of Philip's humility)

q.t: How can you teach others patience, if you are so wanting in patience yourself ? My son, the greatness of our love for God is known by the greatness of our desire to suffer for His love.
q.w: The Life of Saint Philip Neri, by Father Bacci (sayings of the Saint)
q.l: Book II, Chapter XX (Of Philip's patience)

q.t: Nay, say rather that you are not worthy of so great a good, for there is no surer or clearer mark of God's love than adversity.
q.w: The Life of Saint Philip Neri, by Father Bacci (sayings of the Saint)
q.l: Book II, Chapter XX (Of Philip's patience)

q.t: in order to begin well and end better, two things are necessary, — to be devout to the most holy Mother of God, and to hear mass every morning, when there is no legitimate hindrance.
q.w: The Life of Saint Philip Neri, by Father Bacci (sayings of the Saint)
q.l: Book II, Chapter XXI (Of Philip's perseverance and stability in well-doing)

q.t: My children, mortify yourselves in little things, that you may afterwards more easily mortify yourselves in great ones.
q.w: The Life of Saint Philip Neri, by Father Bacci (sayings of the Saint)
q.l: Book II, Chapter XIX (Of the mortifications with which Philip exercised his spiritual children)

q.t: As I have time to pray, I have an assured hope of obtaining from our Lord whatever favour I ask.
q.w: The Life of Saint Philip Neri, by Father Bacci (sayings of the Saint)

q.t: No more, my son, no more; let the devil alone; we do him too much honour by talking about him: put all your trust in Christ and in His most Precious Blood, for He it is who has overcome the devil in you; be at peace, and leave Him to act for you.
q.w: The Life of Saint Philip Neri, by Father Bacci (sayings of the Saint)
q.l: Book II, Chapter VIII (Of the great care which Philip took of his penitents when they were ill)

q.t: You must also love Him fervently, if you would be perfect, for holiness comes from love, and the greater the love, the greater the saint.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XV, To a lady, on what constitutes true holiness

q.t: When you place yourself in God's presence, endeavour rather to listen to Him, than to speak to Him, and strive more to love Him, than to learn from Him.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XVII, To a lady, on confidence in God

q.t: As I have often repeated, God loves you as you are. Be content that His love should come from His goodness, and not from your merits. What does it matter to a bride if she is not beautiful, if the bridegroom's affection for her makes her seem so in his eyes?
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XIV, On scruples, addressed to a lady

q.t: God is so faithful that He never abandons those who have recourse to Him; His love is so tender that far sooner will the sea run dry, or the sun cease shining, than the heavenly Father lack pity for His own.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XXIII, To a devout person, treating of humility, pride, and the perfect love of God

q.t: Take care not to appear empty-handed before our Lord, and think not that you are giving Him anything, if you give not your love. Nothing but God can make you happy, nor can anything you offer Him but yourself satisfy Him.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XXII, To a lady, on the feast of the Epiphany

q.t: Ever keep the cross before your eyes, and unite your heart to Him Who placed Himself upon it. Do not be satisfied until suffering becomes sweet to you, for that is the sign of true love.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter VI, To an invalid lady

q.t: Speak little with men, but much with God in prayer in the depths of your heart, for all good must come to us from Him. He wishes us to obtain it through prayer, and especially to keep before our minds the Passion of Jesus Christ our Lord.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter X, To some friends who were undergoing persecutions

q.t: Look upon all your fellow men as God's creatures, whom He desires to be saved, and you will find that you cannot wish harm to those for whom God has such good will.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter X, To some friends who were undergoing persecutions

q.t: Who can help being inflamed by love on thinking that he is about to receive the Infinite Goodness within his bosom? Who would not tremble with reverential fear in that Presence, before which the powers of heaven are awed? Who would not resolve never to offend Him, but to praise and serve Him evermore?
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter IV, To a priest, on due preparation for saying Mass

q.t: Withdraw your heart from the world before God takes your body from it: keep your mind in perfect peace however much it is occupied in business. A man who is travelling post haste concerning a matter which is of life and death to him, does not turn his head to look at anything as he passes.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter VIII, On preparation for death

q.t: Oh tepidity! If those who give way to it only rightly understood what it is, they would less easily fall victims to it, for they would dread to become the slaves of so cruel a tyrant. If we are free from this vice, nothing we can do or suffer for God, even death itself, seems too great a burden, whereas the victim of tepidity finds a straw too heavy for him to carry.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XIII, To a friend, on tepidity

q.t: Genuine faith believes without the need of argument or miracles; and love trusts its Beloved, even though He chastise it: true patience is content to suffer without relief, and so a real confidence in God remains unshaken by the absence of any solace from Him.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XVII, To a lady, on confidence in God

q.t: whether He consoles or afflicts us, He keeps His holy watch over us, and never so faithfully as when we think He has abandoned us. Trust in God's judgment, dear Sister, and not in your own, since He understands what is best for you, and knows the present and future state of your soul.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XVIII, To console a young lady in great affliction

q.t: No force can prevail with a Father like the tears of his child, nor is there anything which so moves God to grant us, not justice, but mercy, as our sorrow and self-accusation.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XIX, To one of his disciples, teaching him how to lead a good life

q.t: Patience is the guardian of all the other virtues, and, if it fail, we may lose in one moment the labour of many days.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XIX, To one of his disciples, teaching him how to lead a good life

q.t: Live here as a stranger — your body on earth, but your heart above — so that when our Lord calls you, He may not find you sleeping, but ready to go with Him, and to hear the sweet words: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant, enter thou into the joy of thy Lord."
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XIX, To one of his disciples, teaching him how to lead a good life

q.t: God showed that we were dear to Him when He made us after His own image, but far stronger was the proof He gave of His love, when He made Himself in the image of man. He abased Himself to raise us to His level; He became man to make us as gods; He descended from heaven that He might raise us to dwell there with Him, and above all, He died to give us life.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XXI, To a young lady, telling her how to make ready to receive the new-born Jesus

q.t: He has many poor brethren, and those who love Him must love them too, for His sake. Give them your alms, for they are the brothers of your Creator.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XXI, To a young lady, telling her how to make ready to receive the new-born Jesus

q.t: Pride can live in peace with no one, not even with itself, while humility agrees with all men, for it abases itself before everyone and bears patiently with them, believing with all its heart that they are better than itself.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XXIII, To a devout person, treating of humility, pride, and the perfect love of God

q.t: So powerful is the fire of the Holy Spirit, that it mounts upwards, and gives us a love and trust in God that no water of sorrow or affliction can extinguish: it remains ever alight; it fills and inflames our hearts, burning away all evil, so that not even death can conquer him whose evil passions it has destroyed.
q.w: Letters of Blessed John of Avila
q.l: Letter XXIV, To a lady, on the feast of Pentecost

q.t: To conclude, prayer is a bath, an open place, a bed of pleasure, wherein the soul recreateth and refresheth herself.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part I, ch. 1 (the fruit of prayer and meditation), p. 70

q.t: For we see the souls of those who arise from profound and devout prayer, to be strengthened with admirable resolutions, adorned with new graces, and replenished with firm purposes of amendment of life
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer

q.t: Consider, also, the continual motion of our life, never resting night nor day, but goeth forward without ceasing, and every day more and more wasteth itself; so that it may not unfitly be compared to a candle, which, by little and little, consumeth itself, and when it giveth the clearest light, the sooner it approacheth unto its end; also to a flower, which springeth up in the morning, at noon fadeth, and at night wholly withereth away.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part I, ch. 2, Meditation for Tuesday (the miseries of human life), p. 83

q.t: Conjecture, then, the foolish madness of the lovers of this world, who, that they might enjoy one only momentary pleasure of this transitory life, do not fear to expose themselves to the loss of eternity.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part I, ch. 2, Meditation for Tuesday, p. 81

q.t: He that suffered, was God; what he suffered, were the most grievous torments, and such that never any mortal man did endure the like. For whom? for most ungrateful creatures, cursed and worthy of hell fire.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part I, ch. 2, Meditation for Sunday (the benefits of God: redemption), p. 107

q.t: Faith, is the prime root and foundation of a Christian ; hope, is a staff to defend us from all tribulations of this present life ; charity, the end of all perfection; fear of God, the beginning of true wisdom; humility, is the basis and ground work of all virtues; patience, is the strongest armor against the fury of our enemies
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer

q.t: Then for all the members of his mystical body ; for the just, that he would be pleased to conserve them in their sanctity ; for sinners, to convert them from their wicked courses, to the amendment of their lives; for the dead, that he would free them from the expiating torments wherein they are detained, and bring them to their eternal rest.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer

q.t: Therefore, he that will meditate with fruit to his soul, must come to it like an humble simple creature, bringing rather a will disposed to taste these holy mysteries profitably, than acrimony of understanding to discuss them learnedly: for this is proper to those who give themselves to study, not to those who consecrate themselves unto devotion.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part I, ch. 12, Second Document, p. 176

q.t: we must imitate a good rider upon an untoward horse, who neither holdeth him in too hard, nor looseth the reins upon his neck, but guideth him equally, that he giveth not back, nor goeth forward too speedily. So we must strive in meditation, that attention be moderate, diligently resisting evil thoughts, but not violent with anxiety.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part I, ch. 12, Fourth Document, p. 178

q.t: The weak understanding is little able to conceive or comprehend anything of God, but the will can love him very much.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part I, ch. 12, Eighth Document, p. 185

q.t: let him return again to meditation, in which we must behave ourselves like a gardener; who, when he watereth a bed of his garden, after he hath once sprinkled it with water, expecteth awhile, until it be drunk in, then sprinkleth again, that at last it may thoroughly wet the earth, that it may become more fruitful.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part I, ch. 12, Eighth Document, p. 186

q.t: For the spirit of devotion is delicate; which, when it is gone, it hardly returneth again, at least with great difficulty. For as trees and plants must be watered in due season, otherwise they wither away and perish, so devotion, except it be watered with the waters of holy meditation, doth easily vanish.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part II, ch. 3 (nine impediments to devotion), p. 197

q.t: Let him also consider, that we are compassed about with a custody of angels, which do guard us, as well in, as out of prayer ; they assist us carrying up our prayers to heaven ; they help us to bring to nothing the devices of our crafty enemy, and to confound all his mischievous plots.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part II, ch. 4, remedy for the fifth temptation, p. 204

q.t: let him put on the shape of a child, for such our Lord maketh partakers of his divine secrets; let him not mind to search or know the causes of God's works; let him shut the eyes of natural reason, and open the eyes of faith
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part II, ch. 4, remedy for the fourth temptation (against faith), p. 203

q.t: If all things in the world could be known, they are but as nothing ; and, therefore, it is much better to exercise ourselves in the love of God, the fruit whereof remaineth for ever, and in whom we see and know all things.
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part II, ch. 4, remedy for the eighth temptation (inordinate desire of learning), p. 206

q.t: the servant of God that expecteth merit and comfort in the way of perfection, must not fix his eyes so much upon one only virtue, although it be never so rare and excellent, but generally attend to all, as one string upon an instrument maketh no music, except we strike the rest, so one virtue cannot make a spiritual harmony in our souls, if the other be wanting
q.w: A Golden Treatise of Mental Prayer
q.l: Part II, ch. 5, Seventh Admonition, p. 215

q.t: Grant, O my Sovereign Good, that I may write nothing but what may be for Thy greater glory and my own confusion.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: The Blessed Virgin has always taken great care of me. I had recourse to her in all my necessities, and she has preserved me from great dangers.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: I would wish also to make known the greatness of His mercies, for it seemed, as though He had undertaken constantly to pursue me and oppose His goodness to my malice, and His love to my ingratitude.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: I therefore used to hide myself in order to learn how to love my Sovereign Good, Who so strongly urged me to return Him love for love. But I thought that I could never love Him enough no matter what I did, unless I learnt how to meditate.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: In leaving the world, I will do so wholly and entirely and will hide myself in some little nook in order to forget it, to be forgotten by it and to see it no more.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: All I wish for is Thy love and Thy Cross, that suffices for me to become a good religious, which is all I desire.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: O my Lord, I wish for nothing but Thee and am content with the choice Thou wilt make for me.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: by this I understood that I was to give and abandon everything to Him, Who is Power itself, and that one loses nothing by giving Him all.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: In the midst of all my fears and difficulties my heart, nevertheless, was always in a state of unalterable peace.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: But Thou, O my Lord, what hast Thou not done to win the hearts of men, and yet they refuse them to Thee and often drive Thee from them!
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: But, alas! I am unfaithful, I often fail, and He sometimes seemed pleased that I should do so, both to humble my pride and to make me distrust myself, seeing that without Him I could only do evil and would fall continually without being able to rise again.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: I shed an abundance of tears on seeing that His only revenge for my sins and continual infidelities was an excess of love by means of which He seemed to wrestle with my ingratitude.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: I was always equally satisfied whether what I asked for was granted or refused; it was sufficient for me to obey.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: As yet I had been unable to find means to begin the devotion to the Sacred Heart for which alone I lived.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: my one desire was to see His reign established. I, therefore, abandoned to Him the defence of His own cause whilst I suffered in silence.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: I then understood better the grievousness and malice of sin, for which I felt such a horror, that I would have preferred a thousand times to cast myself into hell than to commit a single one wilfully.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: On commencing some exercise, I often felt as though it would be impossible for me to hold out to the end; nevertheless, I began the next with the same difficulty, saying: "O my God, grant me the grace to be able to continue to the end," and I returned thanks to my Sovereign Lord for thus measuring my minutes by the clock of His Passion so that all my hours might strike in unison with His sorrows.
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: I wish for Thee alone, bereft upon the Cross, where I desire to love Thee alone for the love of Thyself. O take all the rest from me, so that I may love Thee without admixture of pleasure or self-interest
q.tr: the Sisters of the Visitation, Walmer

q.t: It is, therefore, true that we are sent, not only to love God, but, moreover, to make others love Him. It is not enough for us to love God if our neighbor, too, do not love Him ; and we cannot love our neighbor as ourselves if we do not procure for him the good we are bound to wish for ourselves, namely, the Divine love which unites us to Him who is our Sovereign Lord.
q.w: Conference to the Missionaries on charity (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: Those who have true charity within show it externally. It is the property of fire to give heat and light, and it is characteristic of love to be communicative. We should love God with all our strength and in the sweat of our brow. We ought to serve our neighbor with our wealth and our life. O, how happy to become poor in charity to others !
q.w: Conference to the Missionaries on charity (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: hence, you, too, must treat the sick poor with gentleness, with pity and love, for they are your lords and masters as well as mine.
q.w: Conference to the Daughters of Charity (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: He has called you to the congregation to serve the poor, and that this service might be the more agreeable He has caused rules to be given you; but if, at the time of the exercises, He calls you elsewhere, go on the instant and do not once doubt but that you do His most holy will.
q.w: Conference to the Daughters of Charity (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: Charity is the soul of all virtues, and the paradise of communities. Yes, the house wherein charity reigns is a paradise, for, where charity is, there God dwells.
q.w: Conference to the Missionaries (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: Who is perfect ? No man on earth. But who is not called imperfect ? Since, then, all men have their faults, all have need of support.
q.w: Conference to the Missionaries on charity (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.l: Ch. X (Charity), §II, third act of charity ('mutual support'), p. 129
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: it is not sufficient to have charity in the heart and in word; it should pass into action, even to the extent of giving, if required, our life, as did our Lord.
q.w: Conference to the Missionaries on charity (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.l: Ch. X (Charity), §II, sixth act of charity, p. 133
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: From this we may perceive that humility, when true and real, introduces all the other virtues into the soul, and that by sincerely and profoundly humbling ourselves, from sinners, that we were, we become just.
q.w: Conference on humility, 18 April 1659 (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: What else can we do but love a person who humbles himself? He is like a valley that receives the moisture of the mountains; he draws down upon himself the blessings and the good will of all.
q.w: Conference to the Missionaries on charity (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.l: Ch. X (Charity), §II, fifth act of charity, p. 132
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: Give me a man of prayer, and he will be capable of everything
q.w: Saying to the Missionaries (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: It is in prayer that a blinded soul recovers its sight, that a soul, deaf to the voice of God, becomes attentive to His holy inspirations, that the soul which was heavy and sluggish in the things of salvation, on account of its evil habits, becomes strong, full of courage and of fervor.
q.w: Conference to the Daughters of Charity on prayer, May 1648 (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: Let us, therefore, persevere in prayer without being discouraged by dryness or difficulties. During twenty years, St. Teresa was unable to make mental prayer, and did not understand it. She, however, persevered, and God imparted to her an eminent gift of prayer.
q.w: Conference to the Daughters of Charity on prayer, May 1648 (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: In regard to Divine things I place no more reliance in human means than I would in the assistance of the Devil. The things of God are done by themselves, and true wisdom consists in following Providence step by step.
q.w: Letters to M. Codoing, 1643-1644 (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.l: Ch. IV (Conformity to the Will of God), §II, p. 30
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: Let us offer ourselves to Him to do and to suffer everything for His glory and for the edification of His Church ; He wants nothing more. If He desires results, they are in His power, not in ours. In His presence let our wills and our hearts expand, ready for anything without determining on any till He shall have spoken.
q.w: Letter (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.l: Ch. IV (Conformity to the Will of God), §II, p. 31
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: Oh ! but it requires little to be a saint ! The most sovereign, and almost only, means is to accustom yourself to do in all things the will of God.
q.w: Letter to Mademoiselle Le Gras (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.l: Ch. IV (Conformity to the Will of God), §II, p. 33
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: There is reason to hope that, as with fruit-trees, so will it be with you; for the more a long and severe winter checks and retards them, the deeper root they take and the more fruit they bear.
q.w: Letter to M. Desdames in Poland, 20 June 1659 (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.l: Ch. IV (Conformity to the Will of God), §II, p. 32
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: Our Lord, in these words, recommends us to make God reign within us, and then to co-operate with Him in extending and enlarging His Kingdom by the conquest of souls.
q.w: Commentary on 'Seek first the Kingdom of God' (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: The Church is the kingdom of God, and He inspires her rulers with principles of good government. His Holy Spirit presides over the councils
q.w: Teaching on faith (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: Let us have confidence in God, gentlemen and my brethren, but let it be entire and perfect, holding it for certain that having once begun His work in us He will finish it.
q.w: Conference to the Missionaries (in Maynard, Virtues and Spiritual Doctrine)
q.l: Ch. II (Hope and Confidence in God), §II, p. 11
q.tr: a Priest of the Congregation of the Mission

q.t: Afflictions, fears, desolations, aridity, abandonments, temptations, and other trials, are an excellent broom, that sweeps from your soul all the dust and mire of the imperfections that are concealed from you.
q.w: Letters (quoted in Strambi, The Life of the Blessed Paul of the Cross)
q.l: Vol. II, Book II, ch. XXV (Sentiments of Father Paul on the value of suffering)

q.t: The remedy in your tribulations is the balsam of the Divine Will, which must be embraced and loved, both in prosperity and adversity.
q.w: Letters (quoted in Strambi, The Life of the Blessed Paul of the Cross)
q.l: Vol. II, Book II, ch. XXV

q.t: I know no better place than to fall asleep, satiated with the Cross, on the sacred Heart of our blessed Saviour, the furnace of holy love.
q.w: Letters (quoted in Strambi, The Life of the Blessed Paul of the Cross)
q.l: Vol. II, Book II, ch. XXV

q.t: When the soul keeps her passions in subjection, when she keeps herself recollected in God, when she walks in lively faith, which form the silence and the midnight that God requires, then the Divine Word is born in the soul by a nativity wholly spiritual, wholly divine.
q.w: Recorded instructions on prayer (in Strambi, The Life of the Blessed Paul of the Cross)
q.l: Vol. II, Book II, ch. X (Of the gift of prayer), explaining 'Dum medium silentium'

q.t: In this divine solitude everything is learned. In this divine interior school, more is learned by being silent, than by speaking. St. Mary Magdalen fell at the feet of Jesus through love, there she was silent, she listened, loved, and even melted with love
q.w: Letters (quoted in Strambi, The Life of the Blessed Paul of the Cross)
q.l: Vol. II, Book II, ch. X (Of the gift of prayer)

q.t: Rules have been given, but God is the Master, let us abandon ourselves to Him, confide in Him, and strip ourselves of all things, and God will clothe us according to his pleasure.
q.w: Letters (quoted in Strambi, The Life of the Blessed Paul of the Cross)
q.l: Vol. II, Book II, ch. X

q.t: God is pleased with those who are little, and who become as little children. He keeps them in His Divine bosom, and nourishes them with that Divine milk of holy love
q.w: Letters (quoted in Strambi, The Life of the Blessed Paul of the Cross)
q.l: Vol. III, Book II, ch. XXXV (His instructions and maxims for the acquisition of holy humility)

q.t: Prayer which humbles the soul, inflames it with love, and stimulates it to virtue and to suffering, is never a delusion.
q.w: Letters (quoted in Strambi, The Life of the Blessed Paul of the Cross)
q.l: Vol. III, Book II, ch. XXXV

q.t: If some dust of imperfection clings to your soul, be not disturbed, but burn and consume it in the fire of the love of God, humbling yourself, and tranquilly repenting, but with a humble, strong, and hearty repentance, and then continue in peace.
q.w: Letters (quoted in Strambi, The Life of the Blessed Paul of the Cross)
q.l: Vol. III, Book II, ch. XXXV

q.t: Love speaks little, and he who loves most speaks least, I mean in holy prayer. The language of love is fire, which burns, liquefies and consumes itself, as a holocaust before God; then the gentle breath of the Holy Spirit stirs up our worthless ashes, and raises them till they are lost in the abyss of the Divinity.
q.w: Letters (quoted in Strambi, The Life of the Blessed Paul of the Cross)
q.l: Vol. I, Book II, ch. I (Of Father Paul's faith)

q.t: We are more certain however, that Almighty God inhabits our souls, than that our arms belong to our bodies, because, in proof of one, we have only the fallible evidence of our senses, while in support of the other, we have the infallible teaching of faith.
q.w: Recorded words to his community (in Strambi, The Life of the Blessed Paul of the Cross)
q.l: Vol. I, Book II, ch. I

q.t: The fear of the Lord is our cross. As then one who is crucified no longer has the power of moving or turning his limbs in any direction as he pleases, so we also ought to affix our wishes and desires--not in accordance with what is pleasant and delightful to us now, but in accordance with the law of the Lord, where it constrains us.
q.l: Book IV, ch. 35 (charge of Abbot Pinufius to a novice, recorded by Cassian)

q.t: From the fear of the Lord arises salutary compunction. From compunction of heart springs renunciation, i.e. nakedness and contempt of all possessions. From nakedness is begotten humility; from humility the mortification of desires. Through mortification of desires all faults are extirpated and decay. By driving out faults virtues shoot up and increase. By the budding of virtues purity of heart is gained. By purity of heart the perfection of apostolic love is acquired.
q.l: Book IV, ch. 43 (recapitulation of Abbot Pinufius' charge)

q.t: For it is not an external enemy whom we have to dread. Our foe is shut up within ourselves: an internal warfare is daily waged by us: and if we are victorious in this, all external things will be made weak, and everything will be made peaceful and subdued for the soldier of Christ.
For it is not so much the corruptible flesh as the clean heart, which is made a shrine for God, and a temple of the Holy Ghost.

The chief part then of our improvement and peace of mind must not be made to depend on another's will, which cannot possibly be subject to our authority, but it lies rather in our own control. And so the fact that we are not angry ought not to result from another's perfection, but from our own virtue, which is acquired, not by somebody else's patience, but by our own long-suffering.
For no one is ever driven to sin by being provoked through another's fault, unless he has the fuel of evil stored up in his own heart.
The end of our profession indeed, as I said, is the kingdom of God or the kingdom of heaven: but the immediate aim or goal, is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end
q.l: Conference I (First Conference of Abbot Moses), ch. 4

q.t: For the gain from fasting will not balance the loss from anger, nor is the profit from reading so great as the harm which results from despising a brother.
For all gifts are given for a time as use and need require, but when the dispensation is ended they will without doubt presently pass away: but love will never be destroyed.

For whatever our mind has been thinking of before the hour of prayer, is sure to occur to us while we are praying through the activity of the memory. Wherefore what we want to find ourselves like while we are praying, that we ought to prepare ourselves to be before the time for prayer.
q.l: Conference IX (First Conference of Abbot Isaac, On Prayer), ch. 3

q.t: We pray within our chamber, when removing our hearts inwardly from the din of all thoughts and anxieties, we disclose our prayers in secret and in closest intercourse to the Lord. We pray with closed doors when with closed lips and complete silence we pray to the searcher not of words but of hearts.
Wherefore we ought to pray often but briefly, lest if we are long about it our crafty foe may succeed in implanting something in our heart.
We can then only ascend to that true perfection when, as He first loved us for the grace of nothing but our salvation, we also have loved Him for the sake of nothing but His own love alone.
q.l: Conference XI (First Conference of Abbot Chaeremon), ch. 7

q.t: Lastly it is a much greater thing to be unwilling to forsake good for good's own sake, than it is to withhold consent from evil for fear of evil.
But it is a clear sign of a soul that is not yet thoroughly purged from the dregs of sin, not to sorrow with a feeling of pity at the offences of others, but to keep to the rigid censure of the judge

You must then, if you want to get at the true knowledge of the Scriptures, endeavour first to secure steadfast humility of heart, to carry you on by the perfection of love not to the knowledge which puffeth up, but to that which enlightens. For it is an impossibility for an impure mind to gain the gift of spiritual knowledge.
q.l: Conference XIV (First Conference of Abbot Nesteros), ch. 10

q.t: Humility therefore is the mistress of all virtues, it is the surest foundation of the heavenly building, it is the special and splendid gift of the Saviour.
q.l: Conference XV (Second Conference of Abbot Nesteros), ch. 7

q.t: For all things, however useful and necessary they seem, should yet be disregarded that disturbing anger may be avoided, and all things even which we think are unfortunate should be undertaken and endured that the calm of love and peace may be preserved unimpaired, because we should reckon nothing more damaging than anger and vexation, and nothing more advantageous than love.
q.l: Conference XVI (First Conference of Abbot Joseph), ch. 7

q.t: Take also John — that is, the grace of God, which stands at the door and knocks, — that it may enlighten thee to the perception of the evils which thou hast done, and may preserve thee in the good which thou hast taken in hand.
q.w: Sermons (tr. J. M. Neale, Mediaeval Preachers)
q.l: Sermon for the Second Sunday in Lent, on the Transfiguration ('Our Lord taking the three Apostles up to Mount…)

q.t: Note that this ladder hath two staves and six steps, by which the ascent is made. The two staves set forth His Divine and Human Natures. The six steps are His humility, poverty, wisdom, patience, mercy, and obedience.
q.w: Sermons (tr. J. M. Neale, Mediaeval Preachers)
q.l: Sermon for the Second Sunday in Lent (Transfiguration), Neale p. 228

q.t: Ye that are of one mind, behold the mast in the middle of the ship; that is to say unanimity of faith and heart in the Church.
q.w: Sermons (tr. J. M. Neale, Mediaeval Preachers)
q.l: Sermon on 1 Peter 3:8 ('Christian virtues compared to the parts of a ship'), Neale p. 236

q.t: The hedgehog is the obstinate sinner, covered all over with the prickles of sins. If you endeavour to convince him of the sin he has committed, he immediately rolls himself up, and hides, by excusing, his fault.
q.w: Sermons (tr. J. M. Neale, Mediaeval Preachers)
q.l: Sermon for the Second Sunday in Lent ('Sinners compared to hedgehogs'), Neale p. 246

q.t: hidden from every human conscience, insomuch that if every man that is in the world were acquainted with the sin of one that has confessed to thee, thou nevertheless art bound to conceal it, and to shut it up under the key of eternal silence.
q.w: Sermons (tr. J. M. Neale, Mediaeval Preachers)
q.l: Second sermon for the First Sunday in Lent ('Confession, a desert'), Neale p. 240

q.t: My lord and father, I place myself entirely in your hands ; do with me what you will ; but I protest to you that I am called by God to the Company of Jesus, and that in resisting this call you resist the will of God.
q.w: Words to his father, the Marquis Ferrante Gonzaga
q.l: Castiglione, 1585 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part I, ch. 6)

q.t: no one can serve two masters, the world and God ; I wish to make sure of my salvation, and I exhort you to do likewise.
q.w: Reply to the vassals of Castiglione
q.l: Castiglione, 1585 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part I, ch. 7)

q.t: Your Highness can, indeed, command men, and they will obey you ; but you cannot command the elements, because they belong to God only, whom your Highness is also bound to obey.
q.w: Words to the Infante Diego of Spain
q.l: Madrid (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part I, ch. 4)

q.t: Because I am poor, and it is to practise poverty I act thus ; the poor must only spend money on necessary things.
q.w: Recorded saying at the Roman College
q.l: Rome (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 3)

q.t: Brother, do not excite yourself, for indeed you are wrong ; we make profession of poverty; so, if he treats us conformably to our profession, we cannot and ought not to complain.
q.w: Words to Brother Giacomo Borlasca at an inn
q.l: Journey to Mantua, 1589 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 5)

q.t: how much better should we be lodged in the naked chambers of our house and on our poor pallets, than amidst all these honours and luxuries.
q.w: Words at the castle of Castel Goffredo
q.l: 1589 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 5)

q.t: I feel like one who, cold and frozen in mid-winter, finds himself laid in a downy, warm bed : even such was the cold from which I suffered when away from our houses, and such is the comfort I experience on finding myself once more within them.
q.w: Words on returning to the college of Milan
q.l: March 1590 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 6)

q.t: But again I entreat your lordship to give heed to this, because everywhere you will find God, whether awaiting repentance or punishing the offences committed against Himself, as also against those who desire to serve Him.
q.w: Letter to his brother Ridolfo Gonzaga
q.l: Milan, 6 February 1590 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 6)

q.t: inasmuch as God transcends all created things, honours, possessions, and all else whatever, so in the like measure ought our inward esteem of His Divine Majesty to surpass all other esteem or conception. But as the finite capacity of our heart does not admit of this, at least we ought to strive that the esteem in which we hold Him be the highest that is possible to us.
q.w: Letter of advice to his brother Ridolfo Gonzaga
q.l: Milan, 17 March 1590 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 6)

q.t: As for your vassals, I will simply observe that God has perhaps given them into your charge in a special and peculiar manner, only in order to signify to you the special and spiritual care which you ought to have of them, recognizing in the Providence of God towards yourself a pattern of the manner in which you ought to provide for them.
q.w: Letter of advice to his brother Ridolfo Gonzaga
q.l: Milan, 17 March 1590 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 6)

q.t: For the rest, I commit it to God to instruct and guide you to our blessed country ; to the which that I may attain with you and others, I have embraced my present state of life.
q.w: Letter of advice to his brother Ridolfo Gonzaga
q.l: Milan, 17 March 1590 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 6)

q.t: as the execution of what I have recommended to you must be the work of Divine grace more than of your own efforts and my exhortations, I offer and promise ever to recommend you in my prayers, such as they are, to His Divine Majesty; and may He preserve and guide you to that happy end to which His elect shall attain.
q.w: Letter of advice to his brother Ridolfo Gonzaga
q.l: Milan, 17 March 1590 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 6)

q.t: I pass my time joyfully, with the hope of being called, before many months are over, from the land of the dead to that of the living, and from the company of men here below to that of the Angels and Saints in Heaven ; in fine, from the sight of these earthly and perishable things to the vision and contemplation of God, in whom is all good.
q.w: Letter to his mother, Donna Marta Tana
q.l: Rome, spring 1591 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 8)

q.t: may God, Ever-Blessed, bless us both, and fulfil your holy desires: pray for me, and I will pray for you.
q.w: Blessing given to the dying Father Luca Corbinelli
q.l: Rome, May 1591 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 8)

q.t: Now if charity, as St. Paul says, makes us weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice, how great, Signora my mother, must be your joy for the favour you receive from God in my person ; God our Lord leading me to true happiness with the assurance of never losing it more.
q.w: Last letter to his mother, Donna Marta Tana
q.l: Rome, 10 June 1591 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 8)

q.t: We shall not be long separated; we shall meet again above, and never more to part ; we shall enjoy together a blissful union with our Redeemer, praising Him with all our powers, and eternally singing His mercies.
q.w: Last letter to his mother, Donna Marta Tana
q.l: Rome, 10 June 1591 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 8)

q.t: firmly persuaded that whatever God does is well done, taking away from us what first He gave, and this only to set it in a place of safety and freedom, and to confer upon it all that we ourselves should wish.
q.w: Last letter to his mother, Donna Marta Tana
q.l: Rome, 10 June 1591 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 8)

q.t: According to your opinion I am a little better ; nevertheless, according to God's will, I shall die this evening.
q.w: Words to the infirmarian on his last day
q.l: Rome, 20 June 1591 (E. H. Thompson, Life of St. Aloysius Gonzaga (1867), Part II, ch. 8)

q.t: Blessed art thou, my Lord, my God, and most beloved lover of my soul, who art one God in three persons. Glory and praise be to thee, O my Lord Jesus Christ, who wast sent by thy Father into the body of a Virgin, yet ever remainest with thy Father in heaven, the Father with his divinity remaining inseparably with thee in thy humanity in the world.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life and Passion of Our Lord
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. I

q.t: Benediction and glory be to thee, my Lord Jesus Christ, who didst wonderfully fast for forty days in the desert, and didst permit thyself to be tempted by thy enemy the devil, whom thou didst drive off by a single word, when so it pleased thee.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life and Passion of Our Lord
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. I

q.t: Eternal benediction be to thee, my Lord Jesus Christ, for each hour in which thou didst endure the most intense bitterness and agony on the cross, for us sinners.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life and Passion of Our Lord
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. I

q.t: Perpetual honor be to thee, my Lord Jesus Christ, who, in such agony, didst humbly look with benign eyes of charity on thy most worthy Mother, who never sinned, nor consented to even the slightest sin, and consoling her, didst faithfully commit her to the guardianship of thy disciple.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life and Passion of Our Lord
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. I

q.t: Blessed be thou, my Lord Jesus Christ, who, for our salvation, didst permit thy side and heart to be pierced with a lance, and didst send forth copiously from the same side thy precious blood and water to redeem us
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life and Passion of Our Lord
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. I

q.t: Eternal honor be to thee, my Lord Jesus Christ, who didst rise from the dead on the third day, and didst manifest thyself alive to such as thou didst wish ; and after forty days, didst ascend in the sight of many to heaven, and didst there honorably place thy friends whom thou hadst delivered from limbo.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life and Passion of Our Lord
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. I
