q.t: Eternal praise and jubilee be to thee, my Lord Jesus Christ, who didst send down thy Holy Spirit into the hearts of thy disciples, and didst augment in their spirits immense divine love.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life and Passion of Our Lord
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. I

q.t: Blessed be thou, and pleased and glorious forever, my Lord Jesus, who sittest on the throne in thy kingdom of heaven, in the glory of thy divinity, living corporally with all thy most holy members, which thou didst assume of the flesh of a Virgin. And thus thou wilt come on the day of judgment to judge the souls of all, living and dead.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life and Passion of Our Lord
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. I

q.t: Blessed and venerated be thou, my Lady Virgin Mary, most holy Mother of God, whose noblest creature thou art, and who was never so closely loved as by thee, O glorious Lady.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life of the Blessed Virgin
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. II

q.t: Praise be to thee, my Lady Virgin Mary, who when thou didst attain an age to know that God, thy Creator, existed, didst immediately begin to love him intensely, above all things, and didst then most discreetly order thy day and night, in different offices and exercises to the honor of God; and didst so curtail the food and sleep of thy glorious body as to be apt to serve God.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life of the Blessed Virgin
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. II

q.t: Blessed be thou, my Lady Virgin Mary, who didst fly to Egypt with thy most holy Son, whom thou didst afterwards bring with joy to Nazareth, and behold him, thy Son, as he increased bodily, humble and obedient to thee and Joseph.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life of the Blessed Virgin
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. II

q.t: Rejoice, especially, my Lady Virgin Mary, and let the whole earth rejoice with thy joy, that thy Son permitted thee to remain many years in this world after his ascension, to console his friends and strengthen them in faith, to help the needy, and sagely counsel the Apostles.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life of the Blessed Virgin
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. II

q.t: Blessed be thou, my Lady Virgin Mary, who from thy ardent charity and maternal love didst unceasingly, hour by hour, desire to go to thy beloved Son, now sitting in heaven; and thou living in this world, by sighing for heavenly things, didst humbly conform thyself to the divine will, whereby, as divine justice dictated, thou didst unspeakably increase thy eternal glory.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life of the Blessed Virgin
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. II

q.t: Then also didst thou understand, that whoso loves God more ardently in this world, will be placed nearer to himself by God, in heaven.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life of the Blessed Virgin
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. II

q.t: Praised then be God, supreme Emperor and Lord, who created thee to so great honor, that thou shouldst become perennially Empress and Lady in the kingdom of heaven, to reign with him eternally through ages of ages. Amen.
q.w: Prayer of Praise and Thanksgiving on the Life of the Blessed Virgin
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. II

q.t: Blessed, therefore, art thou O most blessed Virgin, in whom the mighty God became a little child ; the ancient Lord became a puny infant; the everlasting God and invisible Creator became a visible creature.
q.w: Prayer to the Virgin Mary, temple of Solomon (Revelations, Book III, ch. 29)
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. XXIV, Select Prayers, IV

q.t: Obtain, then, that the infant Solomon who slumbered in thee, watch with me, so that no sinful delight sting me, that the contrition of my sins be permanent, love of the world be dead within me, my patience persevering, my penance fruitful.
q.w: Prayer to the Virgin Mary, temple of Solomon (Revelations, Book III, ch. 29)
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. XXIV, Select Prayers, IV

q.t: Blessed art thou, O my God, my Creator and Redeemer. Thou art the ransom by which we have been redeemed from captivity, by which we are directed to all salutary things, by which we are associated to the unity and trinity.
q.w: Prayer to God the Redeemer and to Mary (Revelations, Book IV, ch. 75)
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. XXIV, Select Prayers, V

q.t: So thou, most sweet mother, didst show to the world its God, whom men had lost, and didst bear him in time who was begotten before time, at whose birth earthly and heavenly things rejoiced.
q.w: Prayer to God the Redeemer and to Mary (Revelations, Book IV, ch. 75)
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. XXIV, Select Prayers, V

q.t: When the Virgin perceived that she had been delivered, she immediately bowed her head, and joining her hands, adored her Son with great respect and reverence, saying: "Welcome, my God, and my Lord, and my Son."
q.w: Vision of the Nativity at Bethlehem (Revelations, Book VII, ch. 21)
q.l: Revelations of St. Bridget (New York: Sadlier, 1862), ch. VIII, The Nativity

q.t: Place your hope and firm trust in God; He will surely help you in every difficulty. Be instant in praying to Him, in humbling yourselves before His Almightiness; for most assuredly, since He hath trusted this undertaking to you, so will He give you strength to carry it out, provided only that you fail Him not.
q.w: Counsels (Ricordi) to the Lady-Counselors of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Opening exhortation, before the First Advice (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIV)

q.t: Whenever you see a weak soul, timid, and disposed to lose hope and heart, comfort her, give her courage, open up to her the bright vision of God's infinite mercies, and enable that shrinking heart to open itself wide to the sweet influences of consolation.
q.w: Counsels (Ricordi) to the Lady-Counselors of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Second Injunction (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIV)

q.t: Of this assured prospect let nothing make them doubt, no matter what may be their trouble or difficulty; for all these little miseries will soon vanish from their path, and be succeeded by serenity and joy; and, then again, the little we may have to endure in this life is as nothing in comparison to the wealth of happiness stored up in Paradise.
q.w: Counsels (Ricordi) to the Lady-Counselors of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Fifth Admonition (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIV)

q.t: Assure them, moreover, of this, — that I shall, by and by, be more truly living, than I was when their eyes beheld me in the body, and that soon I shall see them and know them better, and be better able to help them, inasmuch as I shall be always in their midst with Him who is my Love, who is the Love of all of us.
q.w: Counsels (Ricordi) to the Lady-Counselors of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Fifth Admonition (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIV)

q.t: Whatever, then, you would have them do, that do yourselves first. What weight can your reprehensions or admonitions have, if the fault you would correct is but too apparent in your own conduct?
q.w: Counsels (Ricordi) to the Lady-Counselors of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Sixth Injunction (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIV)

q.t: Take them all to your heart, therefore, and bear with them all tenderly; for you have not been appointed to judge God's handmaidens. He alone knoweth what His own purpose is
q.w: Counsels (Ricordi) to the Lady-Counselors of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Eighth Reminder (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIV)

q.t: The last word of prayer which I address to you, and which I could write with my own blood, is that you continue to be bound together in so sweet and loving a union that all have but one heart and one will.
q.w: Counsels (Ricordi) to the Lady-Counselors of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Last Reminder (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIV)

q.t: Indeed, in these times, so pregnant with danger and with moral pestilence, you can find no better refuge than at the feet of Christ Jesus.
q.w: Counsels (Ricordi) to the Lady-Counselors of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Seventh Reminder (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIV)

q.t: endeavor with the help of God to conceive and cherish in your hearts the purpose of taking on you this charge and its cares for the sole love of God and the pure zeal for the salvation of souls. Thereby the whole course of your labors and government will be like a tree planted and rooted in this twofold love, incapable of bearing any but the sweetest and most healthful fruit.
q.l: First Bequest (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XVI)

q.t: For it is the nature of true motherly love among persons of the world, that if a parent had a thousand sons and daughters, she would have all and each of them perfectly present to her mind and heart. This is the law of love.
q.l: Second Bequest (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XVI)

q.t: Above all, take care never to use compulsion. God hath made us all free-willed, and to no one's free-will doth He do violence. He leads them to obey Him by show of reason, by inviting motives, and by gentle persuasion.
q.l: Third Bequest (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XVI)

q.t: His light and the sweet splendor of His truth shall surround you in the hour of death, and shall deliver you from the hand of the enemy. So, then, persevere joyously and faithfully in the work you have undertaken. Beware, beware, I say, of yielding to tepidity.
q.l: Closing words after the Last Bequest (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XVI)

q.t: My God, I grieve and feel my heart wrung with pain at seeing all these unhappy creatures of Thine, who are so blind as not to know Thee, who have no care of being made sharers in the merits of Thy sacred Passion. Most willingly would I, were it in my power, give my life to have the veil removed from their eyes.
q.w: Rule of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Ch. 5, On Prayer (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIX)

q.t: In this adorable Sacrifice are contained in the most wonderful way all the merits of the Passion of our dear Lord. The greater the attention, the faith, the contrition of the assistants, the greater must be the share they have in these blessed merits, and the deeper the consolation derived therefrom.
q.w: Rule of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Ch. 6, On the Mass (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIX)

q.t: Obedience grounded in charity is, in the soul of man, like a great light, in whose brightness all his works are made good and acceptable.
q.w: Rule of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Ch. 8, On Obedience (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIX)

q.t: Therefore, above all things, let her keep her heart pure, and her conscience free from every evil thought, from every shadow of envy, ill-will, dissension, rash judgment — in a word, from every sinful emotion and desire. On the contrary, let her be joyous, filled with charity, faith, and trust in God.
q.w: Rule of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Ch. 9, On Virginity (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIX)

q.t: let each one set herself about divesting herself of all things, and placing all her wealth, her love, her delight, not in dress, or in eating and drinking, or in her parents and relatives, or in herself or her personal foresight and wisdom ; but in God alone, and in His fatherly and infinitely wise providence.
q.w: Rule of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Ch. 10, On Poverty (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIX)

q.t: as by fasting one mortifies one's bodily appetites and senses, even so by prayer one obtains from God the real gift of spiritual life. Wherefore, considering our constant need of the divine assistance, we should apply mind and heart to the task of praying without intermission.
q.w: Rule of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Ch. 5, On Prayer (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIX)

q.t: Meanwhile, pray, and make others pray, that God may not forsake His Church; but that it may please Him to reform her as best beseemeth Him, and as He shall judge more conducive to our good, to His own greater honor and glory.
q.w: Counsels (Ricordi) to the Lady-Counselors of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Seventh Reminder (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIV)

q.t: Tell them that they must wish to see me, not on earth, but in Heaven, where our Love is. Let them place their hopes on high, not on the things of earth. Let Christ Jesus be their only treasure
q.w: Counsels (Ricordi) to the Lady-Counselors of the Company of St. Ursula
q.l: Fifth Admonition (O'Reilly, St. Angela Merici and the Ursulines (1880), ch. XIV)

q.t: there is something else to do besides heaping up riches, of which no one can guarantee the possession. If you really have at heart the prosperity of your family and the well being of your children, it is in the service of Jesus Christ you must seek these favours.
q.w: Reply to his father (as a novice at Mechlin)

q.t: That my relations had to beg their bread from door to door would not be a trial or a shame to me. That they should offend God mortally, I could not endure.
q.w: Letter to Canon John Froymont, Rome, 23 November 1619 (postscript)

q.t: Now, for seven or eight years, you have proved the miseries of human nature, and have tasted, with Christ Jesus, of the chalice of His bitter Passion. See Him now, standing there at your bedside, with outstretched arms ready to embrace you.
O brother, what joy I feel at seeing the hidden God of our altars so honoured.
q.w: Words to a fellow novice at Mechlin

q.t: I never speak without first thoroughly thinking what I ought to say, and recommending it to God, so as never to say anything that may displease Him.
q.w: Words to a companion at the Roman College

q.t: When you take your cassock into your hands, before putting it on, kiss it, rejoicing in your mind that to-day you are still allowed to wear the livery of Christ.
q.w: Order of the day (written at Rome)

q.t: Put yourself above none, and think highly of every one, because, though your brother now seems to you imperfect, how do you know but that he is chosen by God to be a martyr
q.w: Resolutions for humility against pride (1620), no. 6

q.t: Mind your own defects, not those of others, and consider yourself inferior to all. I will mind seriously what I am bound to do, and not what is done by others.

Have a care about God, and God will have care of you. One who does not value prayer, cannot last out in the spiritual life. I will always be specially attached to spiritual things, above all to meditation, examen, and spiritual reading. Prayer is so displeasing to the devil, that he strives to put every hindrance in its way.

Take great care never to neglect your prayers, or any other exercise of devotion, when this melancholy comes over you, because the devil only seeks to disquiet you that he may bring about his own plans.
q.w: Counsel to a fellow scholastic (Bernardine Victorinus)

q.t: The most powerful and chiefest means that I have used in seeking to gain religious perfection has been love and devotion towards the ever Blessed Virgin, and be you, in like manner, always a true child of Mary.
q.w: Answer to William van Aelst the day before his death (August 1621)

q.t: Thou knowest that Thou art all I ever had, all I have in this life. Do not Thou, then, my Lord Jesus, abandon me
q.w: Prayer before the crucifix during his last illness (night of 10 August 1621)

q.t: Come, brother, let us be glad, let us make ready. This is the best of news, the greatest joy that I could have
q.w: Words to the infirmarian, Brother Ballera, on learning he would receive Viaticum (August 1621)

q.t: There is nothing more pleasing to God than to be helpers of His Son, and to be willing to undertake the charge of saving souls. Our holy mother, the Church, rejoices in nothing more than in those who bring souls again to spiritual life, thereby despoiling hell, defeating the devil, casting out sin, opening heaven, making the angels glad, glorifying the most Holy Trinity, and preparing for themselves a never-fading crown.
q.w: Third sermon to his eleventh diocesan synod
q.l: Giussano, Book VIII, ch. 13 (vol. II, p. 370)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: One single soul is worthy of the presence and guardianship of a Bishop.
q.w: Reply to a cardinal-bishop who would not reside in his small diocese
q.l: Giussano, Book VIII, ch. 13 (vol. II, p. 368)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: The workers must be very zealous for the salvation of souls, purchased by the precious Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. This zeal will be found in them when every one makes every effort possible to prevent the loss of souls ransomed at so great a price.
q.w: Rules for the workers of the Confraternity of Christian Doctrine
q.l: Giussano, Book VIII, ch. 13 (vol. II, p. 371)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: If the people make little progress in serving God, it is the Bishop who is in fault, because he is negligent of the things of their salvation.
q.w: Saying on the duties of a bishop
q.l: Giussano, Book VIII, ch. 10 (vol. II, p. 354)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: It was thus that, by deferring the time of restoration to health, God taught us day by day more and more plainly the vanity of the hopes which many placed in human efforts — taught us also that it was the work of His hand — and by this means pointed out to us the true way of restoration. He did not heal us all at once, that we might know that He required of us perfect conversion and amendment
q.w: Memoriale to the people of Milan after the plague
q.l: Giussano, Book IV, ch. 14 (vol. I, p. 464)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: Praised be the name of the Lord always, and by all, but chiefly by us who have tasted of His loving-kindness.
q.w: Memoriale to the people of Milan after the plague
q.l: Giussano, Book IV, ch. 14 (vol. I, p. 463)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: to be a King is not so great a glory as to live in obedience to the King of Heaven, and to give laws to many subjects is not so high a prerogative as to keep them in obedience to the law of God, and that not by force of arms, but by the spread of His Gospel
q.w: Letter to Stephen Bathory, King of Poland (1583)
q.l: Giussano, Book VII, ch. 3 (vol. II, p. 189)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: In your present rank, you cannot, even if you would, escape the eyes of men. You have been put in this high place that your light may point out the way to those who have lost it, and shine out afar as a beacon to those who know the truth.
q.w: Letter to Cardinal Andrew Bathory on his elevation
q.l: Giussano, Book VII, ch. 3 (vol. II, p. 190)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: Most Holy Father, turn now all your thoughts to your heavenly home, place all your hope in our crucified Lord, who is our resurrection and our life. He is our Advocate, and the Sacrifice offered for our sins.
q.w: Words to his dying uncle, Pope Pius IV (December 1565)
q.l: Giussano, Book I, ch. 12 (vol. I, p. 67)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: Do not be displeased with me, Holy Father. I am now wedded to the spouse whom I have so long desired.
q.w: Reply to Pope Pius IV after his ordination to the priesthood (1563)
q.l: Giussano, Book I, ch. 5 (vol. I, p. 25)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: I wear this red garment to show that in case of need I have to shed my blood in the service of God and for the benefit of Holy Church.
q.l: Giussano, Book VIII, ch. 3 (vol. II, p. 305)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: It gives me the greatest possible comfort and consolation when I am ill, to contemplate the mysteries of the Passion of our Lord, especially the Agony in the Garden, and the Burial.
q.w: Words to Father Francis Panigarola during his last illness (1584)
q.l: Giussano, Book VII, ch. 12 (vol. II, p. 248)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: I do not wish to know of any one who has ill-will against me, because I am going to say Mass shortly, and do not want my peace of mind to be disturbed.
q.w: Reply on being handed proofs of a plot against his life (1579)
q.l: Giussano, Book VIII, ch. 17 (vol. II, p. 396)
q.tr: anonymous (for the Oblates of St. Charles)

q.t: If you do some good thing, even a small thing in its way, and you do it with love and charity, God is very much pleased with it
q.l: Prediche volgari I, 336; Howell, ch. III, p. 282

q.t: By this action Christ our Master teaches us how in prayer we ought to use gestures by which the mind may be moved, and uplifted, as we raise our eyes above, and join our hands, and bend our knees, using outward actions. Not that these outward signs make our prayer more effectual with God, for God is a searcher of hearts and He is not moved by outward signs.
q.l: Opera III, 245; Howell, ch. III, p. 283

q.t: Of all the graces that descend to man, even as God is the general Giver, and Christ the general Mediator, so they are generally dispensed through the glorious Virgin. For she is the neck of our Head, through which all spiritual gifts are communicated to His mystical body.
q.l: Opera II, 54; Howell, ch. III, p. 274

q.t: Do you see those windows over there? One is all open, another half open, another a little way open, another, less. Even into those with their shutters all closed, some of God's grace enters, for there are the chinks. And through every one of those windows some of the sun's brightness enters, but more into some and less into others.
q.l: Prediche volgari II, 205; Howell, ch. III, p. 285

q.t: And though Peter's bark be shaken and tossed about hither and thither, up and down, yet shall the Church endure as long as the world lasts
q.l: Opera III, 157; Howell, ch. III, p. 290

q.t: Jesus, sweet Love, make me feel with what unbounded love thou hast loved us and still dost love us.
q.l: Opera III, 444-445; Howell, ch. IV, p. 321

q.t: Jesus, my Love, grant me fervent love to thee, humble obedience, and thanksgiving, that is, let me have a continual sense of thy benefits and of praising and blessing Thee.
q.l: Opera III, 444-445; Howell, ch. IV, p. 322

q.t: O my Jesus, crucified for me, empty thyself into me and wholly make thyself fast to me with the nails of thy love.
q.l: Opera III, 444-445; Howell, ch. IV, p. 322

q.t: nowadays novelty is better liked than truth and the vain subtlety which rouses astonishment is more willingly listened to than the profitable truth which begets compunction.
q.w: Commentary on the Apocalypse (on ix. 2, 'And the sun was darkened')
q.l: Opera V, 57; Howell, ch. IV, p. 307

q.t: his countenance spoke to me, his gait spoke, and his very silence spoke. The sight of his humility beat down my pride, this contemplation of his calmness repressed my restless spirit.
q.l: Book I, lament for his friend Simon (Dalgairns, ch. V)

q.t: Before thee a Child went, the Child Jesus, showing thee the manger of His poverty, the couch of His lowliness, the chamber of His love, filled with the flowers of His grace, and sprinkled with the unguent of His consolation, and thou didst run after the odour of His ointments.
q.l: Book I, lament for his friend Simon (Dalgairns, ch. V)

q.t: They fear not that tremendous majesty near which they are brought, they have no reverence for that mystic manger, at which they are ministering, where Christ is mystically wrapt in swaddling-clothes, where His most sacred blood is poured in the chalice, where the heavens are opened and angels are standing near, where earthly things are joined with heavenly, and men are the companions of angels.

When thou hast tasted this spiritual sweetness, be not straightway sunk down in sloth, for soon there will rise up by thy side a spiritual enemy, and he is not to be conquered by sloth, but by prayers.

The fire of heavenly love will burn up the yoke of earthly concupiscence, and thou shalt rest in the brightness of wisdom, in the sweetness of heavenly contemplation, and know of a truth that the yoke of the Lord is sweet and his burden light.
But Thy tears, O Lord Jesus, are the excuse for ours, those tears which Thou didst shed for the death of Thy friend, expressing a human feeling, and proving to us Thy charity.
q.l: Book I, lament for his friend Simon (Dalgairns, ch. VI)

q.t: It is necessary then to study the state and the temper of every one who flies hither from the world, to know what is hurtful to each, and to point out to him the best refuge from his enemy.
q.w: Sermons on the Burdens of Isaiah (De Oneribus)
q.l: Sermon 28, preached to his monks at Christmas (Dalgairns, ch. VIII)

q.t: Thus in the nest of discipline must he remain, till he be full fledged, and have the wings of virtue wherewith to fly, for never can he rule, who has not first learned to obey.
q.w: Sermons on the Burdens of Isaiah (De Oneribus)

q.t: And when he shall have learned in the scriptures to refer all his life and knowledge to the love of God and of his neighbour, then on the two wings of wisdom and of love, borne up to the mount of contemplation, let him learn to form this earthly tabernacle after the pattern of the heavenly.
q.w: Sermons on the Burdens of Isaiah (De Oneribus)

q.t: The first step then is conversion, the second purification, the third virtue, the fourth knowledge, the fifth contemplation, the sixth charity. And these perchance are the six steps to the throne of Solomon ; if any one strives to sit thereon, without having trodden them, he will mount, not to take his seat there, but to fall headlong.
q.w: Sermons on the Burdens of Isaiah (De Oneribus)

q.t: In the first of these stages, fear, proceeding from the thought of God's justice, purifies the soul ; and when it is purified, wisdom illuminates it ; and after this illumination the goodness of God rewards it by the infusion of His sweetness.
q.w: On Jesus at Twelve Years Old (De Jesu puero duodenni)

q.t: the Lord hath created two great lights in the firmament of the holy Church, the priesthood and the kingdom. The greater light is the priesthood to rule the day, that is, spiritual things ; the lesser light is the kingdom, to rule the night of worldly things.
q.w: Sermons on the Burdens of Isaiah (De Oneribus)
q.l: Advent sermon on Isaiah 13:10 (Dalgairns, ch. VIII)

q.t: Then shall the moon be turned into blood when the hands of the prince are full of blood, when they take away the right of the just man, and follow not equity, but their own lusts and anger.
q.w: Sermons on the Burdens of Isaiah (De Oneribus)
q.l: Advent sermon on Isaiah 13:10 (Dalgairns, ch. VIII)

q.t: Brethren, I tell you, no misfortune can I suffer, nothing sad or bitter arise, which by the opening of the Holy Scriptures cannot be made to vanish, or be borne with greater ease.
q.l: Sermon preached at the onset of his illness (Dalgairns, ch. VIII)

q.t: But I go to meditate in Thy fields, I turn over the sacred page, then does Thy grace, sweet Jesus, drive away the darkness with its light, do away with weariness, and then do tears succeed to groans, and heavenly joy follows tears.
q.l: Sermon preached at the onset of his illness (Dalgairns, ch. VIII)

q.t: Lo ! my sweet Lord, once I sought rest in the world for my wretched soul, but every where I found toil and groans, grief and affliction of spirit.
q.l: Book I, ch. 28, account of his conversion (Dalgairns, ch. III)

q.t: I began then to consider as much as one who had no experience could do, what great sweetness there is in Thy love, how much peace in that sweetness, how much security in that peace.
q.l: Book I, ch. 28, account of his conversion (Dalgairns, ch. III)

q.t: Put side by side with all our riches, our delights, and honours, this one thing which those who are Christ's possess, the right not to fear death.
q.l: Book I, ch. 28, account of his conversion (Dalgairns, ch. III)

q.t: But Thou, who hearest the groans of the captives, who loosest those appointed unto death, Thou didst burst my chains ; Thou, who bringest publicans and harlots into Paradise, hast converted me, the chief of sinners, to Thyself.
q.l: Book I, ch. 28, account of his conversion (Dalgairns, ch. III)

q.t: I am ready to die for the name of Jesus and the protection of his Church.
q.w: Words at his martyrdom (Edward Grim's account)
q.l: Vol. II, ch. XXXIX, Canterbury Cathedral, 29 Dec. 1170

q.t: Here I am, ready to suffer in the name of Him who redeemed me with his blood ; far be it from me to flee or flinch from what is right for fear of your swords.
q.w: Words at his martyrdom (Edward Grim's account)
q.l: Vol. II, ch. XXXIX, Canterbury Cathedral, 29 Dec. 1170

q.t: It is not right to make a fortress of Christ's church, which is a house of prayer ; it is able to protect its own, even if its doors are open ; and we shall triumph over our enemies by suffering rather than by fighting ; for we came here to suffer, not to resist.
q.w: Words at his martyrdom (Edward Grim's account)
q.l: Vol. II, ch. XXXIX, Canterbury Cathedral, 29 Dec. 1170

q.t: It is of no consequence to me ; for if I am torn limb from limb, I will go. It is now seven years since my church has been deprived of a pastor ; and it is my request, perhaps my last request, to my friends, that if I cannot return to Canterbury alive, they will carry me there dead.
q.l: Vol. II, ch. XXXVIII, on the Flemish coast before his return to England, Dec. 1170

q.t: my cross is the sign of peace, and I will not let it go : the king's sword is an instrument of war
q.w: Recorded sayings at the Council of Northampton

q.t: If we fell at Clarendon, (for all flesh is weak,) we should resume our courage, and again contend with our foe in the strength of God's Holy Spirit. If we pledged ourselves to what was unlawful, you well know that an unlawful oath is not binding.
q.w: Reply to the bishops at the Council of Northampton

q.t: There is no chance left for us, but to arouse Him who is sleeping in the vessel, and say, ' Lord save us, we perish !'
But whither should we flee, save to Him, who is our refuge and our strength ?
But further, when is constancy required, except under persecution ? Are not friends then proved ? If they always yield, how can they ever succeed ? They must one time or other make a stand.

You have consoled them in their distress, which is a great duty of religion : your wealth has relieved their indigence, and the amplitude of your power protected them in their necessities. By such sacrifices God is well pleased, your earthly reputation is amplified and made known, and every blessing is secured to you.
q.w: Letter XXIV, to Matilda, Queen of Sicily

q.t: You ought to have well known that if what your ruler commands is just, you are bound to obey his will ; if unjust, to answer, We must obey God rather than man.
q.w: Letter XXXVII, to the bishops of his province (1166)

q.t: He died for us, leaving us an example, that we may follow his steps. It is ours then to die with Him, to lay down our lives in redeeming His Church from the yoke of slavery, and the oppressions of him who grieves her, the Church, which He hath founded, whose liberty He procured with His own blood
q.w: Letter XXXVII, to the bishops of his province (1166)

q.t: The Church hath ever increased and multiplied under tribulation and blood-shedding. It is her peculiarity to conquer whilst she is injured, to possess understanding when she is refuted, to succeed when she is deserted.
q.w: Letter XXXVII, to the bishops of his province (1166)

q.t: But my hopes are laid up within my own bosom ; for he is not alone with whom the Lord is : when he falls, he shall not be dashed to pieces, for the Lord sustains him in his hand.
q.w: Letter XXXVII, to the bishops of his province (1166)

q.t: Peter was taken from fishing, to become the head of the Church, and, by shedding his blood for Christ, he was thought worthy to receive a crown in heaven, a name of honour upon earth. I pray that we also may do likewise : for we are the successors of Saint Peter, not of Augustus.
q.w: Letter XXXVII, to the bishops of his province (1166)

q.t: We, therefore, utterly cast from us the danger to us and to ours : for he is not to be feared who kills the body, but He who kills both body and soul.
q.w: Letter XXXVII, to the bishops of his province (1166)

q.t: For the Lord does not despise the humble and contrite heart, but embraces it in sincerity. Thus also holy David, after he had offended, humbled himself before the Lord, and asked for mercy, and obtained forgiveness.
q.w: Letter XXXVII, to the bishops of his province (1166)

q.t: Pray for us, that our faith may not fail in tribulation, but that we may say with the apostle, ' Neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor any other creature shall separate us from the love of God.'
q.w: Letter XXXVII, to the bishops of his province (1166)

q.t: For we have rejoiced with no slight joy at the finding of the lost sheep, which the pious shepherd has brought back upon his shoulders to the fold.
q.w: Letter CXII, to William, Bishop of Norwich (Dec. 1170)

q.t: my own soul too doth magnify the Lord, who hath wrought gloriously for us, changing our storm into a favourable wind, and calming the motion of the waves.
q.w: Letter CXII, to William, Bishop of Norwich (Dec. 1170)

q.t: Nothing more lovable could have been commanded. For this sacrament brings about both love and union. For it is a sign of the greatest love to give oneself as food.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke
q.l: On Luke 22:19, 'Do this for a commemoration of me'; Borgnet ed., vol. 23, p. 673
q.o: Nihil etiam amabilius injungi potuit. Hoc enim sacramentum et amoris, et unionis est effectivum. Amoris enim maximi indicium est, seipsum dare in cibum.

q.t: For although the Lord's heart was not cut into pieces, yet the Eucharist, which he gave us out of the great charity of his heart, is no small particle of his heart.
q.w: On the Sacrament of the Eucharist
q.l: De Eucharistia, dist. VI, tract. 1, ch. 2; Borgnet ed., vol. 38, p. 358
q.o: Quamvis enim cor Domini incisum per partes non fuerit, tamen non minima ejus cordis particula est Eucharistia, quam nobis ex tanta cordis sui dedit charitate.

q.t: For the land full of the blessings of all graces is the earthly body of Christ, which he took from the Virgin. This bread grew and was made from the grain of the Trinity in the womb of the Virgin. And it is most plentiful, because in it there is full refreshment of body and soul.
q.w: On the Sacrament of the Eucharist
q.l: De Eucharistia, dist. III, tract. 1, on Isaiah 30:23; Borgnet ed., vol. 38, p. 238
q.o: Terra enim plena benedictionibus omnium gratiarum est terrenum corpus Christi, quod traxit de Virgine. Hic panis crevit et factus est de fruge Trinitatis in utero Virginis. Et est uberrimus : quia corporis et animae est plena in eo refectio.

q.t: For no service is acceptable to God unless it is in the unity of the communion of saints; for what thus gathers into one communion is love, which not only gathers together but makes one.
q.w: On the Sacrament of the Eucharist
q.l: De Eucharistia, dist. IV, ch. 6; Borgnet ed., vol. 38, p. 338
q.o: Servitium enim nullum Deo acceptum est, nisi quod in unitate communionis sanctorum est : id enim quod sic in unam congregat communionem, amor est, non tantum congregativus, sed unitivus.

q.t: So he is a Father who has something of his own in us. Through his creating power he is Father by creation; through the Spirit he is Father by adoption; through the image he is Father by likeness. This Father shows towards us all the right and goodness of a father: for he teaches, corrects, receives, and bestows the treasures of the inheritance.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke
q.l: On Luke 11:2, 'Father'; Borgnet ed., vol. 23, p. 103
q.o: Sic igitur Pater est, qui sui aliquid habet in nobis. Per virtutem creatricem, Pater est creatione : per spiritum autem est Pater adoptione : per imaginem autem Pater assimilatione. Hic Pater omne ad nos ostendit jus et bonitatem patris. Erudit enim, corrigit, recipit, et thesauros confert haereditatis.

q.t: Yet there is one debt which is never to be forgiven but always to be demanded, and so to be paid that it always is and still remains a debt: and this is the debt of charity.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke
q.l: On Luke 11:4, 'forgive us our sins'; Borgnet ed., vol. 23, p. 125
q.o: Est tamen unum debitum quod numquam est dimittendum, sed semper exigendum : et ita reddendum quod semper est et manet adhuc debitum : et hoc est debitum charitatis.

q.t: For in all other things a man makes a sacrifice of what belongs to him; but in temptation he offers himself to God, as Christ offered himself to the Father on the cross.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke
q.l: On Luke 11:4, 'lead us not into temptation'; Borgnet ed., vol. 23, p. 127
q.o: In omnibus enim aliis sacrificium facit homo de suis : in tentatione autem offert seipsum Deo, sicut se Christus in cruce obtulit Patri.

q.t: Therefore not only your head and hands and noble members, but even the hairs of your head, which are the smallest parts and share less in the life of the soul, are all numbered, one by one, so that they cannot be withdrawn from the order of providence.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke
q.l: On Luke 12:7; Borgnet ed., vol. 23, p. 212
q.o: Igitur non tantum caput, et manus, et nobilia membra vestra, sed etiam " capilli capitis vestri, " quae minimae partes sunt, et minus vitam animae participantes, " omnes, " per singula, " numerati sunt, " ne subtrahi possint ab ordine providentiae.

q.t: For the image of God is in us, and the inscription of his name. These two are looked for in a coin, and two others besides, namely purity and weight. So in us, besides the two just named, purity of intention is looked for, and weight of affection or love: whether the image is beautiful, whether the inscription is distinct and clear, whether the intention is pure, whether love is an affection of great weight.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke
q.l: On Luke 20:24, the tribute coin; Borgnet ed., vol. 23, p. 613
q.o: Est enim imago Dei in nobis, et superscriptio sui nominis. Et haec duo quaeruntur in denario, et duo alia, puritas scilicet, et pondus. Sic in nobis praeter duo dicta, quaeritur puritas intentionis, et pondus affectus sive amoris. Si scilicet imago sit pulchra, si superscriptio expressa et clara, si intentio pura, si amor affectus magni ponderis.

q.t: For however laborious the days may be, love does not feel them. Since, then, the proof of love is the showing of the deed (for charity, as Gregory says, does great things if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it is not charity), therefore: If you love me, keep my commandments. His commandment is kept when it is fulfilled in deed.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of John
q.l: On John 14:15; Borgnet ed., vol. 24, p. 539
q.o: Quantumcumque enim laboriosi sunt dies, amor non sentit. Ergo cum probatio dilectionis sit exhibitio operis : charitas enim, ut dicit Gregorius, magna operatur si est : si autem renuit operari, charitas non est. Ergo " si diligitis me, " " Mandata mea servate. " Mandatum ejus servatur quando opere impletur.

q.t: For the speech or word of God, as Augustine says, is knowledge with love. Through love it kindles and inflames the affections, and in them it consumes by purging; through knowledge it enlightens the intellect, and drives the darkness of error and doubt out of the intellect. So it cleanses both, that is, the intellect and the affections.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of John
q.l: On John 15:3, 'Now you are clean by reason of the word'; Borgnet ed., vol. 24, p. 559
q.o: Sermo enim Dei sive verbum, ut dicit Augustinus, est cum amore notitia, et per amorem accendit affectum et incendit, et consumit purgando in affectu : et per notitiam illuminat intellectum, et propellit tenebras erroris, et dubietatis ab intellectu : sic mundat utrumque, intellectum scilicet, et affectum.

q.t: His mother: she alone stood perfectly, so that his mother was entangled in no doubt; she bore within what her Son was suffering outwardly in his body.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of John
q.l: On John 19:25, Mary at the cross; Borgnet ed., vol. 24, p. 659
q.o: " Mater ejus, " quae sola perfecte stetit, ita quod nulla dubietate perplexa fuit mater ejus : intus sustinuit, quod foris in corpore perferebat Filius.

q.t: To these and similar objections it must be answered that in truth one who is an enemy has two things in him: nature, and the vice of enmity. Nature, indeed, is not so depraved that it has nothing good in it or cannot be restored: and for this reason it is to be loved and set right.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke
q.l: On Luke 6:27, 'Love your enemies'; Borgnet ed., vol. 22, p. 428
q.o: Ad haec et similia dicendum, quod in veritate is qui inimicus est, duo in se habet : naturam, et vitium inimicitiarum. Natura quidem non est ita depravata quin aliquid boni habeat, et quin possit reparari : et ad hoc diligenda est et dirigenda.

q.t: He says 'Thou shalt love', not 'Thou shalt know', because the knowledge of God is naturally imprinted on all, and few go astray concerning it; but many go astray concerning love, because whoever loves iniquity or the world is made an enemy of God.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew
q.l: On Matthew 22:37, the greatest commandment; Borgnet ed., vol. 21
q.o: Dicit autem, " diliges : " non cognosces : quia notitia Dei omnibus naturaliter impressa est, et circa illam pauci deviant : sed circa dilectionem multi : quia qui diligit iniquitatem vel mundum, inimicus Dei constituitur

q.t: For nothing is without meaning in so great a Virgin and Mother of God. And if she moved herself from high to higher, let us be ashamed not to rise up from the filth of vices.
q.w: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke
q.l: On Luke 1:39, the Visitation ('Mary rising up'); Borgnet ed., vol. 22, p. 112
q.o: Nihil enim vacat a significatione in tanta Virgine et Dei Matre. Si autem ipsa de alto in altius se egit, pudeat nos a sorde vitiorum non exsurgere.

q.t: There are three things, brethren, three, by which faith stands, devotion holds firm, and virtue endures: prayer, fasting, mercy. What prayer knocks for, fasting obtains, and mercy receives. Prayer, mercy, fasting: these three are one, and they give life to one another. For fasting is the soul of prayer, and mercy is the life of fasting. Let no one tear them apart; they cannot be separated.
q.w: Sermon 43: On Prayer, Fasting and Almsgiving
q.o: Tria sunt, tria, fratres, per quae stat fides, constat devotio, manet virtus. Oratio, jejunium, misericordia. Quod oratio pulsat, impetrat jejunium, misericordia accipit. Oratio, misericordia, jejunium, sunt haec tria unum, dant haec sibi invicem vitam. Est namque orationis anima jejunium; jejunii vita misericordia est. Haec nemo rescindat, nesciunt separari.

q.t: He is a shameless petitioner who asks for himself what he refuses to another. O man, be your own pattern of mercy: in the way you wish, as much as you wish, and as quickly as you wish mercy to be shown to you, just so quickly, so much, and in such a way show mercy to others yourself.
q.w: Sermon 43: On Prayer, Fasting and Almsgiving
q.o: Improbus petitor est, qui quod alii negat sibi postulat. Homo, esto tibi misericordiae forma; sic quomodo vis, quantum vis, quam cito vis, misericordiam tibi fieri; tam cito aliis tantum, taliter ipse miserere.

q.t: But you say: Granted that I can ask, how shall I be able to knock at the secret place of heaven? How? By repeating your prayers, by awaiting the judgement of the Giver, by bearing most patiently the delays of the One who gives; for whoever knocks once and is at once indignant if he has not been heard is not a humble petitioner but an imperious exactor.
q.o: Sed dicis, Esto quod petere possim, pulsare quomodo potero coeleste secretum? Quemadmodum? Iterando preces, et exspectando judicium largitoris, moras dantis patientissime sustinendo; quia quicumque cum semel pulsaverit, indignatur mox si non fuerit auditus, iste non est petitor supplex, sed est imperiosus exactor.

q.t: O man, if you cannot be without sin, and you want everything always to be forgiven you, always forgive. As much as you want to be forgiven, so much forgive; as often as you want to be forgiven, so often forgive; indeed, since you want everything to be forgiven you, forgive everything. O man, understand that by forgiving others you have given pardon to yourself.
q.l: Sermo 67, on 'Forgive us our debts'; Migne, PL 52, col. 392C
q.o: Homo, si sine peccato esse non potes, et vis semper dimitti tibi totum, dimitte semper; quantum vis dimitti tibi, dimitte tantum; quoties vis dimitti tibi, toties tu dimitte; immo quia vis totum dimitti tibi, totum dimitte: homo, intellige quia remittendo aliis tu tibi veniam dedisti.

q.t: I beseech you, he says, by the mercy of God. Paul pleads, or rather God pleads through Paul, because he wishes to be loved more than feared. God pleads because he wishes to be not so much a Lord as a Father. God pleads by mercy so that he may not punish with severity.
q.w: Sermon 108: That Man Should Be Both Sacrifice and Priest to God
q.o: Obsecro, inquit, vos per misericordiam Dei. Rogat Paulus, immo per Paulum rogat Deus, quia plus amari vult quam timeri. Rogat Deus quia non tam Dominus esse vult quam pater. Rogat Deus per misericordiam, ne vindicet per rigorem.

q.t: Love gives birth to desire; it swells with ardour, and ardour presses on towards what is not granted. What more need be said? Love must see what it loves: this is why all the saints counted everything they had merited as little, if they were not to see the Lord.
q.w: Sermon 147: On the Mystery of the Incarnation
q.o: Amor parit desiderium, gliscit ardore, ardor ad inconcessa pertendit. Et quid plura? Amor quod amat non potest non videre: hinc est quod omnes sancti omnia quae meruerant parva duxerunt, si Dominum non viderent.

q.t: O man, why are you so worthless in your own eyes, when you are so precious to God? Why, when you are so honoured by God, do you dishonour yourself in such a way? Why do you ask what you were made from, and not inquire what you were made for? Is not this whole dwelling of the world that you see made for you?
q.w: Sermon 148: On the Mystery of the Incarnation (continued)
q.o: Homo, quare tibi tam vilis es, qui tam pretiosus es Deo? Quare sic honoratus a Deo teipsum taliter inhonoras? Quare quaeris unde factus sis, et ad quid factus sis non requiris? Nonne tota ista quam vides tibi facta est mundi domus?

q.t: She who is called lady by the angel knows and confesses herself a handmaid. For a devout soul, decked with the insignia of favours, grows in obedience: it increases in gratitude; it does not leap up into arrogance or swell into pride. Be it done to me according to thy word. She who believes the word rightly conceives the Word.
q.w: Sermon 142: On the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
q.o: Quae vocatur ab angelo domina, ipsa se cognoscit et confitetur ancillam. Quia devotus animus infulis beneficiorum crescit ad obsequium: augetur ad gratiam, non ad arrogantiam prosilit, non ad superbiam pertumescit. Fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum. Quae credit verbo, merito concipit Verbum

q.t: The Church of Christ is bound together by so close a bond of mutual charity that she is one in many and, by a mystery, whole in each; so much so that the whole universal Church is rightly called the one Bride of Christ, and each single soul, through the mystery of the sacrament, is believed to be the Church in her fullness.
q.w: Book Called "The Lord Be with You" (to Leo of Sitria)
q.o: Ecclesia siquidem Christi tanta charitatis invicem inter se compage connectitur; ut et in pluribus una, et in singulis sit per mysterium tota; adeo ut et omnis universalis Ecclesia non immerito una Christi perhibeatur singulariter sponsa, et unaquaeque anima per sacramenti mysterium plena esse credatur Ecclesia.

q.t: The solitary life is truly a school of heavenly doctrine and a training in the divine arts. For there God is the whole of what is learned, the way along which one presses on, by which one comes to the knowledge of the highest truth.
q.w: Book Called "The Lord Be with You" (to Leo of Sitria)
q.l: ch. 19 (In praise of the solitary life); PL 145, col. 246D
q.o: Solitaria sane vita coelestis doctrinae schola est, ac divinarum artium disciplina. Illic enim Deus est totum, quod discitur; via, qua tenditur, per quam ad summae veritatis notitiam pervenitur.

q.t: The cell is the meeting place of God and men, the crossroads of those who live in the flesh and those who dwell on high. There the citizens of heaven come to converse with men, where it is not so much that tongues of flesh put words together, as that, without any sound of voice, the fruitful secrets of minds are opened. For the cell is the confidant of the secret counsel that God holds with men.
q.w: Book Called "The Lord Be with You" (to Leo of Sitria)
q.l: ch. 19 (In praise of the solitary life); PL 145, col. 248B-C
q.o: Cella nempe est conciliabulum Dei et hominum, compitum in carne degentium, et supernorum. Illuc siquidem superni cives ad colloquia humana conveniunt, ubi non tam linguae carnis verba componunt, quam sine vocis strepitu fecunda mentium arcana patescunt. Cella namque conscientia est secreti consilii, quod habet cum hominibus Deus.

q.t: Therefore, dearest and sweetest brother, while you are hemmed in by blows, while you are chastened by the strokes of heaven's discipline, let no despair weigh down your mind, no murmuring complaint break out, no sorrowful grief swallow you up, no faintness of heart make you impatient; but let there always be serenity in your face, cheerfulness in your mind, and thanksgiving ringing on your lips.
q.l: book 8, letter 6 (to G., a nobleman, in affliction); PL 144, col. 474C
q.o: Quapropter, charissime et dulcissime frater, dum verberibus cingeris, dum coelestis disciplinae tunsionibus castigaris, non mente desperatio deprimat, non querela murmurationis erumpat, non tristitiae moeror absorbeat, non impatientem pusillanimitas reddat; sed semper serenitas in vultu, hilaritas in mente, gratiarum actio resultet in ore.

q.t: Those who are rich, then, are commanded to be stewards rather than owners, and they ought not to regard what they have as their own; for they did not receive passing goods in order to abound in luxuries or to spend them on their own uses, but to carry out the office of administrators while they remain in the stewardship entrusted to them.
q.w: On Almsgiving (to Bishop Mainard of Urbino)
q.o: Qui ergo divites sunt, dispensatores potius jubentur esse, quam possessores: et non proprii juris debent deputare quod habent, quia non ad hoc bona transitoria perceperunt, ut deliciis affluant, vel in proprios haec usus insumant, sed ut administrationis fungantur officio, dum in commisso permanent villicatu.

q.t: Persevere in brotherly charity; in eager love for one another, stand together with one mind against the snares of the ancient enemy. Let the whole structure of your holy work rise upon the foundations of charity; let every building you raise be joined together out of the living stones of the virtues by the mortar of sincere love.
q.l: ch. 24 (A call to all to strive for charity); PL 145, col. 326C-D
q.o: In fraterna charitate persistite, in mutui amoris studio adversus antiqui hostis insidias unanimiter conspirate. Tota sanctae operationis vestrae machina in charitatis se basibus erigat; omne, quod construitis aedificium, ex vivis virtutum lapidibus sincerae dilectionis glutino coalescat.

q.t: So water is born of fire, and fire in turn is begotten of water. For from the fire of divine love springs the grace of compunction, and again from the compunction of tears the ardour of heavenly desire grows. Each depends on the other, and each supplies the other: from the love of God flows the compunction of tears, and through tears our mind burns more fervently with the love of God.
q.l: ch. 13 (Compunction is born of the love of God, and the love of God grows from compunction); PL 145, col. 311A-B
q.o: Ergo et ex igne aqua nascitur, et ex aqua ignis invicem procreatur. Quia videlicet et ex igne divini amoris gratia compunctionis oritur, et rursus ex compunctione lacrymarum desiderii coelestis ardor augetur. Alterum siquidem pendet ex altero et sibimet utrumque invicem praestat, dum et ex amore Dei lacrymarum compunctio profluit, et rursus per lacrymas ad amorem Dei mens nostra ferventius inardescit.

q.t: This is the sum of every holy soul set free from the bonds of the world, and on this its whole intention must be fixed: that through the growth of all its works it should press on to the love of God, and one day rest with delight in the embrace of the true Bridegroom.
q.w: Instruction for a Nun (to the Countess Blanche)
q.o: Et haec est summa cujuslibet sanctae animae mundi nexibus expeditae atque hic tota versari debet intentio, ut ad amorem Dei per omnium suorum operum incrementa contendat, et quandoque in veri Sponsi delectabiliter amplexibus requiescat.

q.t: There they drink from the fountain of life while they thirst, and thirst while they drink; for there neither can eager longing give birth to pain, nor fullness turn to weariness.
q.w: Instruction for a Nun (to the Countess Blanche)
q.l: ch. 15 (On the everlasting bliss of the heavenly Jerusalem); PL 145, col. 748D
q.o: Illic vitae fontem et sitientes hauriunt, et haurientes sitiunt; quia ibi non potest, vel aviditas passionum gignere, vel satietas fastidire.

q.t: O you, whoever you are, turn your heart, that den of foxes, into the hidden mortar of chaste meditation, in which you should never cease to grind fine the manna of the heavenly word, so that from it bread tempered with oil may come forth for you. For the bread tempered with oil is the understanding of Holy Scripture, seasoned with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit.
q.l: ch. 4 (How God rests in us); PL 145, col. 720A-B
q.o: O tu quisquis es, cor tuum, spelaeum scilicet vulpium, in arcanum castae meditationis verte mortarium: in quo videlicet manna coelestis eloquii non desinas subtiliter terere, ut oleatus ex eo panis tibi valeat provenire. Panis enim oleatus sacrae Scripturae est intellectus, Spiritus sancti suavitate conditus.

q.t: But we who seek a jubilee, that is, rest, in God must ourselves offer God a jubilee within us. For whoever does not allow God to rest in his heart in this life will not afterwards be granted by him the rest of the heavenly life.
q.l: ch. 4 (How God rests in us); PL 145, col. 719C
q.o: Sed qui Jubilaeum Deo, hoc est requiem, quaerimus, et ipsi Jubilaeum Deo in nobis exhibere debemus. In cujus enim corde Deus in hac vita requiescere non permittitur, ei postmodum coelestis vitae requiem non largitur.

q.t: Saturday, the Sabbath, whose name means rest, the day on which God is said to have rested, is quite fittingly dedicated to the most blessed Virgin. For she is the house that Wisdom hath built herself, and in her, through the mystery of the lowliness he took upon himself, he rested as on a most sacred couch. Fitting honour is paid to her, and those who pay it are without doubt provided with the help of a sure defence.
q.w: On the Benefit of Prayers for the Dead, and Various Miracles
q.l: ch. 4 (Why Saturday is dedicated to the Blessed Virgin); PL 145, col. 565D-566A
q.o: Sabbatum enimvero, quod requies interpretatur, quo videlicet die Deus requievisse legitur, satis congrue beatissimae Virgini dedicatur. Quam nimirum sibi Sapientia domum aedificavit, atque in ea per humilitatis assumptae mysterium, velut in sacratissimo lectulo requievit. Cui profecto condignus honor impenditur, exhibentibus procul dubio certae defensionis auxilium providetur.

q.t: Yet this skill of human art, whenever it is applied to the handling of the sacred words, must not arrogantly seize for itself the right of mastery, but, like a handmaid to her mistress, should serve with dutiful obedience, lest, if it goes ahead, it go astray, and while it follows the logic of outward words, lose the light of inner power and the straight path of truth.
q.w: On Divine Omnipotence (to Abbot Desiderius of Monte Cassino)
q.l: ch. 5 (On the use of philosophy in sacred disputations); PL 145, col. 603C-D
q.o: Quae tamen artis humanae peritia, si quando tractandis sacris eloquiis adhibetur, non debet jus magisterii sibimet arroganter arripere; sed velut ancilla dominae quodam famulatus obsequio subservire, ne si praecedit, oberret, et dum exteriorum verborum sequitur consequentias, intimae virtutis lumen et rectum veritatis tramitem perdat.

q.t: For almighty God there is no yesterday or tomorrow, but an everlasting today; from him nothing flows away, to him nothing is added; in him nothing changes, nothing differs from himself. That today is eternity, unchangeable, unfailing, unapproachable, to which nothing can be added and from which nothing can be taken away; and all that with us slips away, or changes with the turns of time, stands with him in that today and endures unmoved.
q.w: On Divine Omnipotence (to Abbot Desiderius of Monte Cassino)
q.o: Omnipotenti itaque Deo non est heri, vel cras, sed hodie sempiternum, cui nihil defluit, nihil accedit; cui nihil est varium, nihil a se diversum. Illud hodie aeternitas est incommutabilis, indefectiva, inaccessibilis, cui videlicet nihil addi, nihil valet imminui: et omnia quae apud nos elabendo discurrunt, aut per temporum vicissitudines se variant, apud illum hodie stant et immobiliter perseverant.

q.t: What wonder is it, then, if almighty God, who is the physician of souls, so orders our lives by the hidden art of his governance that he makes medicines for us out of wounds dealt by others, so that when an enemy's wound is inflicted on us, from that very wound the antidote of salvation is prepared?
q.w: On Patience under the Persecution of the Wicked (to Dominic and the hermits of a neighbouring mountain)
q.l: ch. 1 (Patience is the queen of virtues); PL 145, col. 792B
q.o: Quid igitur mirum, si Deus omnipotens, qui est medicus animarum, sic nos occulta sui moderaminis arte disponit, ut ex alienis vulneribus nobis medicamenta conficiat, quatenus dum nobis hostile vulnus infligitur, ex eo potissimum salutis antidotum procuretur.

q.t: Therefore God, from all eternity, in order to share the infinite treasures of his goodness and to show forth his infinite love, ordained this mystery of the divine Incarnation, so that Christ might be great and sit as king at the right hand of God: He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the most High.
q.w: Mariale (Sermons on the Virgin Mother of God)
q.l: Sermons on 'Missus est', Sermon 1 (On the mystery of the Incarnation, willed before all things), §6
q.o: Deus ergo ab aeterno ad communicandos infinitos thesauros bonitatis suae, ad ostendendam infinitam caritatem suam, sacramentum hoc divinae Incarnationis ordinavit, ut Christus esset magnus, et sederet rex ad dexteram Dei: Hic erit magnus, et filius Altissimi vocabitur.

q.t: Christ is the foundation of all creation, of all grace and of all glory, because he is the end of all things, for whose sake all things were created.
q.w: Mariale (Sermons on the Virgin Mother of God)
q.l: Sermons on 'Missus est', Sermon 1 (On the mystery of the Incarnation, willed before all things), §5
q.o: Fundamentum Christus est totius creaturae, totius gratiae et totius gloriae, quoniam finis est omnium, propter quem omnia creata sunt.

q.t: Sorrow is born of love, and love itself, weighed in a just balance, is the measure of sorrow. From great love great sorrow arises. Whoever loves most grieves most when he loses what he loved.
q.w: Mariale (Sermons on the Virgin Mother of God)
q.l: Sermons on the Vision of St. John (Lenten Saturdays), Sermon 6 (On the sorrows of the Virgin Mother of God, Saturday…)
q.o: Oritur ex amore dolor, amorque ipse aequa lance est mensura doloris. Ex magno amore magnus dolor exoritur. Qui maxime amat, is maxime dolet, cum id quod amabat amittit.

q.t: In her, faith and charity were most perfect; but virtue perfects nature, it does not destroy it. Virtue of soul did not keep her from being by nature a woman with a loving, gentle, tender and sweet heart, nor from being a true and natural parent, most loving, a most sweet and tender mother, moved with a mother's deepest feeling toward her only and most beloved Son.
q.w: Mariale (Sermons on the Virgin Mother of God)
q.l: Sermons on the Vision of St. John (Lenten Saturdays), Sermon 6 (On the sorrows of the Virgin Mother of God, Saturday…)
q.o: Perfectissima in ea erat fides et caritas, sed virtus perficit naturam, non destruit. Non efficiebat virtus animi quin mulier esset natura pio, molli, tenero dulcique corde; quin vera et naturalis esset amantissima parens, dulcissima ac tenerrima mater, maternis visceribus affecta erga unicum ac dilectissimum Filium.

q.t: The Holy Scriptures had promised a prince most glorious, most happy, most blessed, wholly divine, true God; there appeared a man able to suffer, mortal, poor, lowly, pitiable. He was the true Son of God, but this did not appear, because the Godhead lay hidden in the humanity.
q.w: Mariale (Sermons on the Virgin Mother of God)
q.l: Sermons on 'Beatus venter', Sermon 3 (On the surpassing blessedness of the Virgin Mother of God), §5
q.o: Promissus fuerat in Scripturis Sanctis princeps gloriosissimus, felicissimus, beatissimus, totus divinus, verus Deus; apparuit homo passibilis, mortalis, pauper, humilis, miserabilis. Erat verus Filius Dei, sed non apparebat, quoniam Divinitas in humanitate latebat

q.t: How sweet is the name of mother! It cannot be told, it cannot be grasped. But the most Blessed Virgin is called not only Mother, but Mother of mercy, that is, most merciful, a most clement Mother, a most tender Mother, most loving.
q.w: Mariale (Sermons on the Virgin Mother of God)
q.l: Sermons on the 'Salve Regina', Sermon 2 (On the opening of the invocation: the power and mercy of the Virgin), §3
q.o: Quam dulce est nomen matris! Dici non potest, comprehendi non potest. Virgo autem Beatissima non solum Mater, sed Mater misericordiae dicta est, hoc est, misericordissima, Mater clementissima, Mater tenerrima, amantissima.

q.t: Let us therefore run to her in our needs, for, upheld by divine authority, she can, and, moved by divine charity, she wills to help us, knowing that it was for our sake that she was so enriched.
q.w: Mariale (Sermons on the Virgin Mother of God)
q.l: Sermons on the Assumption, Sermon 3 (On the holiness and exaltation of the Virgin Mother of God), §4
q.o: Ad ipsam igitur recurramus in nostris necessitatibus, quia, divina auctoritate fulta, potest, et, divina caritate affecta, vult nobis prodesse, sciens quod nostri causa sic ditata est.

q.t: For all holiness consists in charity, which is the bond of perfection; and the perfection of charity consists in the perfect love of God and of neighbour.
q.w: Mariale (Sermons on the Virgin Mother of God)
q.l: Sermons on the Assumption, Sermon 2 (On the Virgin honoured by silence and on her twofold charity), §4
q.o: Nam omnis sanctitas in caritate consistit, quae est vinculum perfectionis, caritatis autem perfectio in perfecta dilectione Dei et proximi

q.t: It came to pass in the eleven hundred and forty-first year of the incarnation of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, when I was forty-two years and seven months old: a fiery light of the greatest brilliance came from the open heaven and poured through my whole brain, and it set my whole heart and my whole breast aflame, like a flame that does not burn but warms, as the sun warms anything on which it sends its rays.
q.l: Book I, Preface (her account of her call); PL 197, col. 383B
q.o: Actum est in millesimo centesimo quadragesimo primo Filii Dei Jesu Christi incarnationis anno, cum quadraginta duorum annorum septemque mensium essem, maximae coruscationis igneum lumen aperto coelo veniens, totum cerebrum meum transfudit, et totum cor totumque pectus meum velut flamma non tamen ardens, sed calens ita inflammavit, ut sol rem aliquam calefacit super quam radios suos immittit.

q.t: Dry and stony ground brings forth thorns and other useless weeds; so too an ill-fitting abstinence, which keeps no just measure and no right order, lays low a person's flesh, because the greenness of fitting nourishment is not given to it. And so the person withers. Where this happens, the winged virtues will surely perish, namely humility and charity, the most beautiful of flowers, because excessive abstinence lacks the greenness of the virtues.
q.l: Letter 98, her reply to Abbess M. of Wechterswinkel (on discretion in abstinence; words she gives as spoken by the Living Light)
q.o: Et sicca terra quae saxosa est germinat spinas atque alias inutiles herbas; sic incongrua abstinentia, quae non habet justum modum et rectum statum, prosternit carnem hominis, quia non datur ei viriditas justae refectionis. Unde etiam homo arescit. Ubi hoc est, certe ibi peribunt volatiles virtutes, scilicet humilitas et charitas pulcherrimorum florum, quoniam nimia abstinentia caret viriditate virtutum

q.t: When Christ Jesus, the true Son of God, hung on the wood of his passion, the Church, joined to him in the secret of the heavenly mysteries, was endowed with his crimson blood. She herself shows this when she often approaches the altar and asks back her dowry, and watches most attentively with what devotion her children receive the divine mysteries as they draw near.
q.l: Book II, Vision 6 (words of the voice from heaven); PL 197, col. 510A
q.o: Christo Jesu vero Filio Dei in ligno passionis suae pendente; Ecclesia in secreto supernorum mysteriorum ipsi associata, purpureo sanguine ejus dotata est. Sicut et ipsa demonstrat; cum frequenter ad altare accedens dotem suam reposcit, et quanta devotione filii ejus ad divina mysteria accedentes ea percipiant, attentissime considerat.

q.t: I, the Almighty, when the offering of bread and wine is presented on the altar dedicated to my name in memory of the Son, wondrously illumine it with my power and glory and transform it into the body and blood of my Only-begotten. How? By the very miracle by which my Son took flesh from the Virgin, this offering too becomes his flesh and blood in this consecration.
q.l: Book II, Vision 6 (words of God the Father as she heard them in the vision); PL 197, col. 529D
q.o: Ego Omnipotens, cum oblatio panis et vini super altare nomini meo dedicatum in memoria Filii oblata fuerit, eam mirabiliter virtute et gloria mea illustrans, in corpus et sanguinem Unigeniti mei transfundo. Quomodo? Ipso miraculo quo Filius meus carnem ex virgine suscepit: etiam oblatio haec in consecratione ista caro et sanguis ejus efficitur.

q.t: Therefore let no one despair over the weight of his iniquities, for whoever despairs of my mercy will not rise again to life. But whoever wrestles with despair and at last brings it to nothing has set himself free, for, standing strong, he has conquered valiantly.
q.l: Book II, Vision 6 (words of God as she heard them in the vision); PL 197, col. 549C
q.o: Quapropter nemo de ponderibus iniquitatis suae desperet, quoniam si de misericordia mea desperaverit, ad vitam non resurget. Qui autem cum desperatione certaverit, et tandem eam ad nihilum deduxerit, hic se liberavit, quia fortis existens viriliter vicit.

q.t: O most sweet branch, budding from the stock of Jesse, O what a great power it is that the Godhead looked upon a most beautiful daughter, as the eagle fixes its eye upon the sun, when the Father on high beheld the Virgin's radiance and willed that his Word should take flesh in her. For when the Virgin's mind was enlightened in the mystic mystery of God, a wondrously bright flower came forth from that Virgin.
q.l: Book III, Vision 13 (song to holy Mary in the heavenly symphony); PL 197, col. 730C
q.o: O tu suavissima virga frondens de stirpe Jesse, o quam magna virtus est quod divinitas in pulcherrimam filiam aspexit, sicut aquila in solem oculum suum figit, cum supernus Pater claritatem virginis attendit, quando verbum suum in ipsa incarnari voluit. Nam in mystico mysterio Dei illustrata mente virginis, mirabiliter clarus flos ex ipsa virgine prodiit.

q.t: O most noble greenness, rooted in the sun, you who shine in bright serenity in a wheel that no earthly excellence can grasp: you are encircled by the embraces of the divine mysteries. You glow red like the dawn and burn like the flame of the sun.
q.l: Book III, Vision 13 (song to the virgins in the heavenly symphony); PL 197, col. 732B
q.o: O nobilissima viriditas quae radicas in sole et quae in candida serenitate luces in rota, quam nulla terrena excellentia comprehendit: tu circumdata es amplexibus divinorum mysteriorum. Tu rubes ut aurora, et ardes ut solis flamma.

q.t: Praise must be given to the Creator on high with the unceasing voice of heart and mouth, for by his grace he places in the heavenly seats not only those who stand upright, but also those who fall and are bowed down.
q.l: Book III, Vision 13 (words of the voice from the shining air); PL 197, col. 735B
q.o: Laudes superno Creatori incessabili voce cordis et oris dandae sunt: cum ipse non solum stantes et erectos, sed etiam cadentes et curvatos in supernis sedibus sua gratia collocat.

q.t: Yet my tabernacle is there where the Holy Spirit pours out his watering. What does this mean? I am in the midst. How? Whoever lays hold of me worthily will fall neither into height, nor into depth, nor into breadth. What does this mean? Because I am that Love whom blazing pride does not cast down, nor deep falls shatter, nor the breadth of evils crush.
q.l: Book III, Vision 13 (closing words of the voice of God); PL 197, col. 738B
q.o: Sed tabernaculum meum ibi est, ubi Spiritus sanctus irrigationem suam perfundit. Quid hoc? Ego in medio sum. Quomodo? Quicunque digne me apprehendit, hic nec in altitudinem, nec in profunditatem, nec in latitudinem incidet. Quid hoc? Quia ego sum charitas illa, quam nec flagrans superbia dejicit, nec profundi casus perfringunt, nec latitudo malorum conterit.

q.t: God, who created all things, made man to his own image and likeness, and marked in him both the higher and the lower creatures; and he held him in such love that he destined him for the place from which the falling angel had been cast out, and ordained him for the glory and honour which that angel had lost in blessedness.
q.w: Book of Divine Works (Liber divinorum operum)
q.l: Part I, Vision 1, ch. 3 (words of the voice from heaven); PL 197, col. 744C
q.o: Deus, qui omnia creavit, hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem suam fecit, et in ipso tam superiores quam inferiores creaturas signavit, eumque in tanta dilectione habuit, ut in locum de quo ruens angelus ejectus erat, destinaret, et ad gloriam et honorem, quem ille in beatitudine perdiderat, ordinaret

q.t: I will not study on dead skins while men are dying of hunger.
q.w: Testimonies of the Bologna Canonization Process (1233)
q.l: Testimony of Brother Stephen, prior provincial of Lombardy, n. 45 (Acta Sanctorum Aug. I, p. 637).
q.o: Nolo studere super pelles mortuas, et homines moriantur fame

q.t: Holy Father, because I have gladly persevered in thy will, and those whom thou gavest me I have kept and preserved, I commend them to thee: preserve them and keep them.
q.w: Testimonies of the Bologna Canonization Process (1233)
q.l: Testimony of Brother Ventura of Verona, prior of Bologna, n. 9 (Acta Sanctorum Aug. I, p. 630).
q.o: Pater sancte, quia libenter perstiti in voluntate tua, et illos, quos dedisti mihi, custodivi et conservavi, ego recommendo eos tibi, conserva et custodi eos.

q.t: Do not weep, for I shall be more useful to you in the place where I am going than I have been here.
q.w: Testimonies of the Bologna Canonization Process (1233)
q.l: Testimony of Brother Rudolph of Faenza, n. 42 (Acta Sanctorum Aug. I, p. 636).
q.o: Nolite plorare, quia ego utilior ero vobis ad locum, ad quem vado, quam hic fuerim.

q.t: I am not worthy of the glory of martyrdom; I have not yet deserved that death.
q.w: Jordan of Saxony, Booklet on the Beginnings of the Order of Preachers
q.l: Vita auctore B. Jordano, n. 25 (Acta Sanctorum Aug. I, p. 545).
q.o: Non ego martyrii dignus sum gloria; nondum merui mortem istam.

q.t: I want to give you the weapons with which you must fight against the devil for the whole of your life.
q.w: Testimonies of the Bologna Canonization Process (1233)
q.l: Testimony of Brother Stephen, prior provincial of Lombardy, n. 46 (Acta Sanctorum Aug. I, p. 637).
q.o: Ego volo dare tibi arma, cum quibus toto tempore vitae tuae debeas pugnare contra diabolum.

q.t: Do you want to abandon poverty so soon, and build great palaces?
q.w: Testimonies of the Bologna Canonization Process (1233)
q.l: Testimony of Brother Stephen, prior provincial of Lombardy, n. 50 (Acta Sanctorum Aug. I, p. 638).
q.o: Vultis tam cito paupertatem relinquere, et magna palatia aedificare?

q.t: I am worthy of being deposed, because I am useless and remiss.
q.w: Testimonies of the Bologna Canonization Process (1233)
q.l: Testimony of Brother Rudolph of Faenza, n. 41 (Acta Sanctorum Aug. I, p. 636).
q.o: Ego sum dignus depositione, quia ego sum inutilis et remissus

q.t: Far be it that I should be buried anywhere but beneath the feet of my brothers.
q.w: Testimonies of the Bologna Canonization Process (1233)
q.l: Testimony of Brother Ventura of Verona, prior of Bologna, n. 8 (Acta Sanctorum Aug. I, p. 630).
q.o: Absit, quod ego sepeliar, nisi sub pedibus Fratrum meorum

q.t: Brother, I have sinned, because I spoke publicly before the brothers about my virginity, which I ought not to have said.
q.w: Testimonies of the Bologna Canonization Process (1233)
q.l: Testimony of Brother Ventura of Verona, prior of Bologna, n. 5 (Acta Sanctorum Aug. I, p. 629).
q.o: Frater ego peccavi, quia publice dixi de virginitate mea coram Fratribus, quod non debuissem dixisse

q.t: What benefit and what delight the solitude and silence of the desert bring to those who love them, only those who have experienced it know. For here strong men may return into themselves as much as they wish and dwell with themselves, diligently cultivate the seeds of the virtues, and feed happily on the fruits of paradise.
q.l: provost of Reims, written from his hermitage in Calabria, n. 684 (Acta Sanctorum Oct. III, p. 616)
q.o: Quid vero solitudo heremique silentium amatoribus suis utilitatis jucunditatisque conferat, norunt hi solum, qui experti sunt. Hic namque viris strenuis tam redire in se licet, quam libet; et habitare secum, virtutumque germina instanter excolere, atque de paradisi feliciter fructibus uti.

q.t: Here one gains that eye whose clear gaze wounds the Bridegroom with love, the eye by which, when it is clean and pure, God is seen. Here a busy leisure is kept, and one rests in quiet activity.
q.l: provost of Reims, written from his hermitage in Calabria, n. 684 (Acta Sanctorum Oct. III, p. 616)
q.o: Hic oculus ille conquiritur, cujus sereno intuitu vulneratur Sponsus amore, quo mundo et puro conspicitur Deus. Hic otium celebratur negotiosum, et in quieta pausatur actione.

q.t: Here, in return for the toil of the struggle, God gives his athletes the reward they long for: the peace that the world does not know, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
q.l: provost of Reims, written from his hermitage in Calabria, n. 685 (Acta Sanctorum Oct. III, p. 616)
q.o: Hic pro certaminis labore repensat Deus athletis suis mercedem optatam, pacem videlicet, quam mundus ignorat, et gaudium in Spiritu S.

q.t: For what is more perverse, what so contrary to reason, to justice and to nature itself, than to love the creature more than the Creator? What, then, do you think should be done, my dearest? What but to yield to the counsels of God, to yield to the truth, which cannot deceive?
q.l: provost of Reims, n. 686 (Acta Sanctorum Oct. III, p. 617)
q.o: Quid enim est perversius, quid tam rationem, justitiam ipsamque naturam oppugnans, quam creaturam plus diligere quam Factorem ? Quid ergo agendum censes, charissime? Quid nisi divinis cedere consiliis, cedere veritati, quae fallere non potest?

q.t: Is it not the worst of labours, and a useless one, to be pulled this way and that by desire, and to be tormented without ceasing by cares and anxieties, by fear and sorrow, for the things one desires?
q.l: provost of Reims, n. 686 (Acta Sanctorum Oct. III, p. 617)
q.o: Nonne pessimus et inutilis est labor, concupiscentia distendi, sollicitudinibus et anxietatibus, timore et dolore, pro concupitis incessanter affligi?

q.t: Flee, then, my brother, flee all these troubles and miseries, and pass over from the storm of this world to the safe and quiet anchorage of the harbour.
q.l: provost of Reims, n. 686 (Acta Sanctorum Oct. III, p. 617)
q.o: Fuge ergo, frater mi, fuge has molestias et miserias omnes, et transfer te a tempestate hujus mundi in tutam et quietam portus stationem.

q.t: And who would not see how beautiful, how profitable and how delightful it is to abide in his school under the discipline of the Holy Spirit, and to acquire that divine philosophy which alone gives true happiness?
q.l: provost of Reims, n. 686 (Acta Sanctorum Oct. III, p. 617)
q.o: Quod quam pulchrum, quam sit utile, quamque jucundum in schola ejus sub disciplina Spiritus S. manere, divinam adipisci philosophiam, quae sola dat beatitudinem veram, quis non videat?

q.t: For you know by what promise you are bound, and how almighty and how fearsome is he to whom you vowed yourself as a pleasing and wholly acceptable offering; to him it is neither lawful nor profitable to lie. For he does not suffer himself to be mocked with impunity.
q.l: provost of Reims, reminding him of the vow they had made together to become monks, n. 687…
q.o: Scis namque, qua sponsione obligatus es, et quam omnipotens est ac terribilis sit, cui temetipsum munus gratum et omnino acceptabile devovisti; cui nec mentiri licet, nec expedit. Nec enim patitur inulte se irrideri.

q.t: For to turn to your own use the goods of others, of which you are the steward and not the owner, is (if I may say so with your leave) as hateful as it is unjust.
q.l: provost of Reims, n. 688 (Acta Sanctorum Oct. III, p. 618)
q.o: Aliena namque, quorum minister sis et non possessor, in proprios usus convertere (ut pace tua dicam) tam est odiosum, quam iniquum.

q.t: Rejoice that you have escaped the many dangers and shipwrecks of this storm-tossed world. Rejoice that you have reached the quiet and safe anchorage of a more hidden harbour, which many desire to reach, and many even strive for with no small effort, and yet do not attain.
q.l: Letter from Calabria to his brothers at the Grande Chartreuse, n. 679 (Acta Sanctorum Oct. III, p. 614)
